body.text:
nāgārjunīyaṃ
madhyamakaśāstram |
body.translated_text:
<s>Nāgārjuna</s>'s
<s>Madhyamakaśāstra</s> (Treatise on the Middle Way)

body.text: ācāryacandrakīrtiviracitayā prasannapadākhyavyākhyayā saṃvalitam | 1
body.translated_text: Together with the commentary called <s>Prasannapadā</s> (Clear Words) composed by <s>Ācārya Candrakīrti</s>. 1

body.text:
pratyayaparīkṣā nāma prathamaṃ prakaraṇam |
āryamañjuśriye kumārabhūtāya namaḥ |
body.translated_text:
The first chapter, named 'Examination of Conditions' (<s>Pratyayaparīkṣā</s>).
Homage to the noble <s>Mañjuśrī</s>, the youthful one (<s>kumārabhūta</s>)!

children.translated_text: He whose dwelling is purified by the abandonment of the two extremes, who is born from the ocean of a perfectly awakened mind, /
who out of compassion taught the profound nature of the waters of the true <s>Dharma</s> as he had realized it. // 1 //
The blazing light of whose vision, using the doctrines of rival debaters as fuel, /
burns to this day the darkness in the minds of the world. // 2 //
Whose unequaled torrents of arrows of knowledge and speech strike down the entire army of the ocean of existence, /
bestowing the glory of sovereignty over the three realms upon the world of disciples together with the gods. // 3 //

children.text: nāgārjunāya praṇipatya tasmai tatkārikāṇāṃ vivṛtiṃ kariṣye |
children.translated_text: Having bowed to that <s>Nāgārjuna</s>, I shall compose a commentary on his <s>kārikās</s> (verses), /
bound together with sentences of clear and true procedure, undisturbed by the wind of sophistry — lucid (<s>prasanna</s>). // 4 //

body.text: tatra 'na svato nāpi parato na dvābhyām'; ityādi vakṣyamāṇaṃ śāstram | tasya kāni saṃbandhābhidhānaprayojanāni iti praśne, madhyamakāvatāravihitavidhinā advayajñānālaṃkṛtaṃ mahākaruṇopāyapuraḥsaraṃ prathamacittotpādaṃ tathāgatajñānotpattihetumādiṃ kṛtvā yāvadācāryanāgārjunasya viditāviparītaprajñāpāramitānīteḥ karuṇayā parāvabodhārthaṃ śāstrapraṇayanam, ityeṣa tāvacchāstrasya saṃbandhaḥ-
body.translated_text: Therein, the treatise to be expounded beginning with 'neither from itself nor from another, nor from both' and so forth — when the question arises: what are its connection (<s>saṃbandha</s>), subject matter (<s>abhidheya</s>), and purpose (<s>prayojana</s>)? — the connection of the treatise is as follows: beginning with the first generation of the mind of awakening (<s>prathamacittotpāda</s>), which is the cause of the arising of the <s>Tathāgata</s>'s knowledge, adorned with non-dual knowledge, preceded by the means of great compassion, established through the procedure set forth in the <s>Madhyamakāvatāra</s>, up to <s>Ācārya Nāgārjuna</s>'s understanding of the unerring purport of the <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s> — out of compassion, for the purpose of instructing others, the composition of the treatise.

children.translated_text: That which teaches you to destroy the enemies of afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) without remainder, and that which rescues from lower rebirths and from existence — /
this teaching and this quality of protection, this pair is not found in other doctrines. //

body.text: iti | svayameva cācāryo vakṣyamāṇasakalaśāstrābhidheyārtha saprayojanamupadarśayan, tadaviparītasaṃprakāśatvena māhātmyamudbhāvya tatsvabhāvāvyatirekavartine paramagurave tathāgatāya śāstrapraṇayananimittakaṃ praṇāmaṃ kartukāma āha-
body.translated_text: Thus. The <s>Ācārya</s> himself, showing that the entire subject matter to be expounded in the treatise is endowed with purpose, and having displayed its greatness by virtue of its being a flawless exposition of that very nature — wishing to pay homage, occasioned by the composition of the treatise, to the supreme teacher the <s>Tathāgata</s> who abides inseparably from that nature — says:

children.translated_text: Without cessation, without arising, without annihilation, without permanence, /
without unity of meaning, without plurality of meaning, without coming, without going — //

body.text: yaḥ pratītyasamutpādam
body.translated_text: that <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> (dependent origination)

body.text: ityādi | tadatrānirodhādyaṣṭaviśeṣaṇaviśiṣṭaḥ pratītyasamutpādaḥ śāstrābhidheyārthaḥ | sarvaprapañcopaśamaśivalakṣaṇaṃ nirvāṇaṃ śāstrasya prayojanaṃ nirdiṣṭam |
body.translated_text: — thus, herein, <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> qualified by the eight distinguishing attributes beginning with 'non-cessation' is the subject matter (<s>abhidheya</s>) of the treatise. <s>Nirvāṇa</s>, characterized as the pacification of all conceptual elaboration (<s>prapañca</s>) and as auspicious (<s>śiva</s>), is indicated as the purpose (<s>prayojana</s>) of the treatise.

body.text: taṃ vande vadatāṃ varam |
body.translated_text: I bow to him, the best of speakers. /

body.text: ityanena praṇāmaḥ | ityeṣa tāvacchokadvayasya samudāyārthaḥ ||
body.translated_text: — by this, the homage is expressed. This, then, is the combined meaning of the pair of verses. //

body.text: avayavārthastu vibhajyate | tatra niruddhirnirodhaḥ | kṣaṇabhaṅgo nirodha ityucyate | utpādanamutpādaḥ | ātmabhāvonmajjanamityarthaḥ | ucchittirucchedaḥ | prabandhavicchittirityarthaḥ | śāśvato nityaḥ | sarvakāle sthāṇurityarthaḥ | ekaścāsāvarthaścetyekārtho 'bhinnārthaḥ | na pṛthagityarthaḥ | nānārtho bhinnārthaḥ | pṛthagityarthaḥ | āgatirāgamaḥ, viprakṛṣṭadeśāvasthitānāṃ saṃnikṛṣṭadeśāgamanam | nirgatirnirgamaḥ, saṃnikṛṣṭadeśāvasthitānāṃ viprakṛṣṭadeśagamanam | etirgatyarthaḥ, pratiḥ prāptyarthaḥ | upasargavaśena dhātvarthavipariṇāmāt-
body.translated_text: The meaning of the individual terms is now analyzed. Therein: <s>niruddhi</s> is <s>nirodha</s> (cessation). Momentary destruction is called <s>nirodha</s>. <s>Utpādana</s> is <s>utpāda</s> (arising) — meaning the emergence of an entity (<s>ātmabhāva</s>). <s>Ucchitti</s> is <s>uccheda</s> (annihilation) — meaning the severance of the continuum (<s>prabandha</s>). <s>Śāśvata</s> means <s>nitya</s> (permanent) — meaning standing firm at all times. <s>Ekārtha</s> means 'of one meaning,' i.e., of undifferentiated meaning — meaning 'not distinct.' <s>Nānārtha</s> means 'of different meanings,' i.e., of differentiated meaning — meaning 'distinct.' <s>Āgati</s> is <s>āgama</s> (coming) — the arrival at a proximate location of those situated at a distant location. <s>Nirgati</s> is <s>nirgama</s> (going) — the departure to a distant location of those situated at a proximate location. The root <s>i</s> has the sense of 'going'; <s>prati</s> has the sense of 'attaining.' Due to the transformation of the root-meaning by the force of the prefix —

children.translated_text: By the prefix, the meaning of the root is forcibly led elsewhere, /
just as the sweetness of the <s>Gaṅgā</s>'s water is altered by the water of the ocean. //

body.text: pratītyaśabdo 'tra lyabantaḥ prāptāvapekṣāyāṃ vartate | samutpūrvaḥ padiḥ prādurbhāvārtha iti samutpādaśabdaḥ prādurbhāve vartate | tataśca hetupratyayāpekṣo bhāvānāmutpādaḥ pratītyasamutpādārthaḥ ||
body.translated_text: The word <s>pratītya</s> here is an absolutive (<s>lyabanta</s>) used in the sense of 'having attained,' i.e., 'in dependence upon.' The root <s>pad</s> prefixed with <s>samut</s> has the sense of 'manifestation' — thus the word <s>samutpāda</s> is used in the sense of 'manifestation.' Therefore, the arising of entities in dependence on causes and conditions (<s>hetupratyaya</s>) is the meaning of <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>.

body.text: apare tu bruvate- itirgamanaṃ vināśaḥ | itau sādhava ityāḥ | pratirvīpsārthaḥ | ityevaṃ taddhitāntamityaśabdaṃ vyutpādya prati prati ityānāṃ vināśināṃ samutpāda iti varṇayanti | teṣāṃ "pratītyasamutpādaṃ vo bhikṣavo deśayiṣyāmi", "yaḥ pratītyasamutpādaṃ paśyati sa dharma paśyati" ityevamādau viṣaye vīpsārthasya saṃbhavāt samāsasadbhāvācca syājjyāyasī vyutpattiḥ | iha tu "cakṣuḥ pratītya rūpāṇi ca utpadyate cakṣurvijñānam" ityevamādau viṣaye sākṣādaṅgīkṛtārthaviśeṣe cakṣuḥ pratītyeti pratītyaśabda ekacakṣurindriyahetukāyāmapyekavijñānotpattāvabhīṣṭāyāṃ kuto vīpsārthatā? prāptyarthastvanaṅgīkṛtārthaviśeṣe 'pi pratītyaśabde saṃbhavati- prāpya saṃbhavaḥ, pratītya samutpāda iti | aṅgīkṛtārthaviśeṣe 'pi saṃbhavati- cakṣuḥ pratītya, cakṣuḥ prāpya, cakṣū rūpaṃ cāpekṣyeti vyākhyānāt | taddhitānte cetyaśabde "cakṣuḥ pratītya rūpāṇi ca utpadyate cakṣurvijñānam" ityatra pratītyaśabdasyāvyayatvābhāvāt samāsāsadbhāvācca vibhaktiśrutau satyāṃ cakṣuḥ pratītya vijñānaṃ rūpāṇi ca iti nipātaḥ syāt | na caitadevam | ityavyayasyaiva lyabantasya vyutpattirabhyupeyā |
body.translated_text: Others, however, say: <s>iti</s> means 'going' or 'perishing.' Those who go in the sense of <s>iti</s> are called <s>itāḥ</s>. <s>Prati</s> has the distributive sense (<s>vīpsā</s>). Thus, having derived the word <s>iti</s> as a secondary derivative (<s>taddhitānta</s>), they explain: <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> means 'the arising of those which perish one after another.' For them, since the distributive sense is possible and since the compound exists in contexts such as 'I shall teach you dependent origination, monks' and 'He who sees dependent origination sees the <s>Dharma</s>' — that derivation might seem stronger. But here, in contexts such as 'Dependent on the eye and visible forms, eye-consciousness arises,' where a specific meaning is directly accepted — the word <s>pratītya</s> in 'dependent on the eye' — even in a single arising of consciousness from a single eye-faculty as cause, which is the desired meaning, how can there be a distributive sense? However, the sense of 'attaining' is possible even where no specific meaning is accepted — 'having attained, there is arising' is <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>. It is also possible where a specific meaning is accepted — as explained: 'dependent on the eye' means 'having attained the eye,' 'in dependence on the eye.' And if the word <s>iti</s> were a secondary derivative, then in 'Dependent on the eye and visible forms, eye-consciousness arises,' since the word <s>pratītya</s> would not be indeclinable, and since the compound would not exist, given that an inflected ending would be heard, the construction would have to be: 'eye-consciousness dependent on the eye and visible forms' — a mere apposition. But this is not so. Therefore, the derivation as an indeclinable absolutive (<s>lyabanta</s>) alone should be accepted.

body.text: yastu- "vīpsārthatvātpratyupasargasya, eteḥ prāptyarthatvāt, samutpādaśabdasya ca saṃbhavārtha tvāt, tāṃstān pratyayān pratītya samutpādaḥ prāpya saṃbhava ityeke | prati prati vināśināmutpādaḥ pratītyasamutpāda ityanye"- iti paravyākhyānamanūdya dūṣaṇamabhidhatte, tasya parapakṣānuvādākauśalatvameva tāvatsaṃbhāvyate | kiṃ kāraṇam? yo hi prāptyarthaṃ pratītyaśabdaṃ vyācaṣṭe, nāsau pratiṃ vīpsārthaṃ vyācaṣṭe, nāpyetiṃ prāptyartham, kiṃ tarhi pratiṃ prāptyartham, samuditaṃ ca pratītyaśabdaṃ prāptāveva varṇayati ||
body.translated_text: As for the one who, having paraphrased the rival's explanation — 'because the prefix <s>prati</s> has a distributive sense, because the root <s>i</s> has the sense of attaining, and because the word <s>samutpāda</s> has the sense of arising: having attained each of those conditions, the arising is <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> according to some; the arising of those which perish one after another is <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> according to others' — and then states a refutation: first of all, his lack of skill in paraphrasing the rival position is to be suspected. For what reason? He who explains the word <s>pratītya</s> in the sense of 'attaining' does not explain <s>prati</s> in the distributive sense, nor does he explain <s>i</s> in the sense of attaining. Rather, he explains <s>prati</s> in the sense of attaining, and explains the combined word <s>pratītya</s> only in the sense of attaining.

body.text: tena idānīṃ prāpya saṃbhavaḥ pratītyasamutpāda ityevaṃ vyutpāditena pratītyasamutpādaśabdena yadi niravaśeṣasaṃbhavipadārthaparāmarśo vivakṣitaḥ, tadā tāṃ tāṃ hetupratyayasāmagrīṃ prāpya saṃbhava pratītya samutpāda iti vīpsāsaṃbandhaḥ kriyate | atha viśeṣaparāmarśaḥ, tadā cakṣuḥ prāpya rūpāṇi ceti na vīpsāyāḥ saṃbandha iti || evaṃ tāvadanuvādākauśalamācāryasya ||
body.translated_text: Therefore, now, with the word <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> derived as 'having attained, there is arising,' if the intention is to refer to every possible object-referent of the word 'arising,' then the distributive connection is made: 'having attained this or that assemblage of causes and conditions, there is arising — <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>.' But if the intention is to refer to a specific referent, then in 'having attained the eye and visible forms,' there is no connection with the distributive sense. Thus far, the <s>Ācārya</s>'s lack of skill in paraphrasing.

body.text:
etadvā ayuktam | kiṃ ca | ayuktametat "cakṣuḥ pratītya rūpāṇi ca utpadyate cakṣurvijñānam" iti, atrārthadvayāsaṃbhavāt iti yaduktaṃ dūṣaṇam, tadapi nopapadyate | kiṃ kāraṇam? kathamanenaiva tatprāpteḥ saṃbhava iti yuktyanupādānena pratijñāmātratvāt | athāyamabhiprāyaḥ syāt arūpitvādvijñānasya cakṣuṣā prāptirnāsti, rūpiṇāmeva tatprāptidarśanāditi, etadapi na yuktam, 'prāptaphalo 'yaṃ bhikṣuḥ'; ityatrāpi prāptyabhyupagamāt | prāpyaśabdasya ca apekṣyaśabdaparyāyatvāt |
prāptyarthasyaiva ācāryāryanāgārjunena pratītyaśabdasya
body.translated_text:
This, too, is incorrect. Moreover, the objection raised as a refutation — that this 'Dependent on the eye and visible forms, eye-consciousness arises' does not admit of both senses — is also untenable. For what reason? How is this established, since it is a mere assertion without adducing a reason, stating that 'having attained that, there is arising'? If the intended meaning were this — that since consciousness is formless, there is no physical contact (<s>prāpti</s>) with the eye, because such contact is seen only among material things — this too is not correct, because contact is accepted even in 'This monk has attained the fruit.' And because the word <s>prāpya</s> (having attained) is synonymous with <s>apekṣya</s> (in dependence on).
Indeed, the <s>Ācārya Ārya Nāgārjuna</s> himself accepts the word <s>pratītya</s> in the sense of 'attaining':"

body.text: tattatprāpya yadutpannaṃ notpannaṃ tatsvabhāvataḥ |
body.translated_text: Whatever has arisen having attained this or that [condition] has not arisen from its own nature. /

body.text: ityabhyupagamāt | tato dūṣaṇamapi nopapadyate ityapare ||
body.translated_text: " — from this acceptance, the refutation too is untenable, according to others. //

body.text: yaccāpi svamataṃ vyavasthāpitam- "kiṃ tarhi, asmin sati idaṃ bhavati, asyotpādādidamutpadyate, iti idaṃpratyayatārthaḥ pratītyasamutpādārtha iti", tadapi nopapadyate, pratītyasamutpādaśabdayoḥ pratyekamarthaviśeṣānabhidhānāt, tadvyutpādasya ca vivakṣitatvāt ||
body.translated_text: As for the establishment of his own view — 'Rather, the meaning of <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> is the meaning of conditionality (<s>idaṃpratyayatā</s>): "this existing, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises"' — this too is untenable, because the individual word-meanings of <s>pratītya</s> and <s>samutpāda</s> are not expressed, and because their derivation is intended.

body.text: athāpi rūḍhiśabdaṃ pratītyasamutpādaśabdamabhyupetya araṇyetilakādivadevamucyate, tadapi nopapannam, avayavārthānugatasyaiva pratītyasamutpādasya ācāryeṇa
body.translated_text: Even if one were to accept the word <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> as a conventional term (<s>rūḍhiśabda</s>), speaking thus like <s>araṇyetilaka</s> (forest sesame) and similar terms — this too is not tenable, because the <s>Ācārya</s> himself accepts <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> as having the meaning consistent with its component parts:

body.text: tattatprāpya yadutpannaṃ notpannaṃ tatsvabhāvataḥ |
body.translated_text: Whatever has arisen having attained this or that [condition] has not arisen from its own nature. /

body.text: ityabhyupagamāt | atha
body.translated_text: " — from this acceptance. Now, if one were to explain:

body.text: asminsatīdaṃ bhavati hrasve dīrghaṃ yathā sati |
body.translated_text: This existing, that comes to be — just as, when the short exists, the long exists. /

body.text: iti vyākhyāyamānena nanu tadevābhyupagataṃ bhavati, hrasvaṃ pratītya, hrasvaṃ prāpya, hrasvamapekṣya dīrghaṃ bhavatīti | tataśca yadeva dūṣyate tadevābhyupagamyate iti na yujyate | ityalaṃ prasaṅgena ||
body.translated_text: " — is not the very same thing thereby accepted? The short having been attained, having reached the short, in dependence on the short, the long comes to be. And therefore, what is being refuted is itself being accepted — this is inconsistent. But enough of this digression. //

body.text: tadevaṃ hetupratyayāpekṣaṃ bhāvānāmutpādaṃ paridīpayatā bhagavatā ahetvekahetuviṣamahetusaṃbhūtatvaṃ svaparobhayakṛtatvaṃ ca bhāvānāṃ niṣiddhaṃ bhavati, tanniṣedhācca sāṃvṛtānāṃ padārthānāṃ yathāvasthitaṃ sāṃvṛtaṃ svarūpamudbhāvitaṃ bhavati | sa evedānīṃ sāṃvṛtaḥ pratītyasamutpādaḥ svabhāvenānutpannatvād āryajñānāpekṣayā nāsminnirodho vidyate yāvannāsminnirgamo vidyate ityanirodhādibhiraṣṭābhirviśe ṣaṇairviśiṣyate | yathā ca nirodhādayo na santi pratītyasamutpādasya tathā sakalaśāstreṇa pratipādayiṣyati ||
body.translated_text: Thus, by the <s>Bhagavān</s> illuminating the arising of entities as dependent on causes and conditions, the following positions are rejected: that entities arise without a cause, from a single cause, from an unequal cause, or that they are created by self, other, both, or neither. And from the rejection of these, the conventional nature of conventional things (<s>saṃvṛti</s>) is revealed as it actually stands. That very conventional <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>, because it is not arisen by its own nature and therefore, from the standpoint of noble knowledge (<s>āryajñāna</s>), there is no cessation in it, up to no going — it is distinguished by the eight distinguishing attributes beginning with 'non-cessation.' And how cessation and the rest do not exist in <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> — this will be demonstrated throughout the entire treatise.

body.text: anantaviśeṣaṇasaṃbhave 'pi pratītyasamutpādasya aṣṭānāmevopādānameṣāṃ prādhānyena vivādāṅgabhūtatvāt | yathāvasthitapratītyasamutpādadarśane sati āryāṇāmabhidheyādilakṣaṇasya prapañcasya sarvathoparamāt, prapañcānāmupaśamo 'sminniti sa eva pratītyasamutpādaḥ prapaḥcopaśama ityucyate | cittacaittānāṃ ca tasminnapravṛttau jḥānajḥeyavyavahāranivṛttau jātijarāmaraṇādiniravaśeṣopadravarahitatvāt śivaḥ | yathābhihitaviśeṣaṇasya pratītyasamutpādasya deśanākriyayā īpsitatamatvāt karmaṇā nirdeśaḥ ||
body.translated_text: Although infinite distinguishing attributes of <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> are possible, only eight are taken up because these are principally the points of contention in debate. When <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> is seen as it truly is, for the noble ones there is a complete cessation of conceptual elaboration (<s>prapañca</s>) whose characteristic is the subject matter and the rest. Since conceptual elaborations cease therein, that very <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> is called the 'pacification of conceptual elaboration' (<s>prapañcopaśama</s>). And since the mind and mental factors do not operate therein, and since the transactions of knowledge and the knowable cease, it is 'auspicious' (<s>śiva</s>) because it is free from all calamities such as birth, old age, death, and so forth. Since the teaching of <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> qualified by the attributes described above is the most desired object of the action, the indication is made by the instrumental case (i.e., by the act of teaching).

children.translated_text: Without cessation, without arising, without annihilation, without permanence, /
without unity of meaning, without plurality of meaning, without coming, without going. // 1 //
That <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> (dependent origination), the pacification of conceptual elaboration (<s>prapañcopaśama</s>), auspicious (<s>śiva</s>) — /
which the Perfectly Awakened One (<s>Sambuddha</s>) taught — to him, the best of speakers, I bow. // 2 //

body.text: yathopavarṇitapratītyasamutpādāvagamācca tathāgatasyaivaikasyāviparītārthavāditvaṃ paśyan sarvaparapravādāṃśca bālapralāpānivāvetya atīva prasādānugata ācāryo bhūyo bhagavantaṃ viśeṣayati- vadatāṃ varamiti ||
body.translated_text: And from the understanding of <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> as described above, seeing that only the <s>Tathāgata</s> alone speaks without distortion of meaning, and comprehending all rival doctrines as mere prattle of fools — the <s>Ācārya</s>, filled with exceeding devotion, further distinguishes the <s>Bhagavān</s>: 'the best of speakers.'

body.text: atra ca nirodhasya pūrvaṃ prativedhaḥ utpādanirodhayoḥ paurvāparyāvasthāyāḥ siddhayabhāvaṃ dyotayitum | vakṣyati hi-
body.translated_text: And here, the mention of cessation (<s>nirodha</s>) first is to indicate the non-existence of a fixed temporal sequence between arising and cessation. For he will say:

children.translated_text: If birth were first and old age and death were subsequent, /
then birth would be without old age and death, and one would be born immortal. //

body.text: iti | tasmānnāyaṃ niyamo yat pūrvamutpādena bhavitavyaṃ paścānnirodheneti ||
body.translated_text: Therefore, there is no such fixed rule that arising must come first and cessation afterwards.

body.text: idānīmanirodhādiviśiṣṭapratītyasamutpādapratipipādayiṣayā utpādapratiṣedhena nirodhādi pratiṣedhasaukarya manyamāna ācāryaḥ prathamamevotpādaprativedhamārabhate | utpādo hi paraiḥ parikalpyamānaḥ svato vā parikalpyeta, parataḥ, ubhayataḥ, ahetuto vā parikalpyeta | sarvathā ca nopapadyata iti niścityāha-
body.translated_text: Now, the <s>Ācārya</s>, wishing to demonstrate <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> as qualified by 'non-cessation' and the rest, considering that by refuting arising the refutation of cessation and the rest will be easy, begins with the refutation of arising itself first. For arising, as conceived by opponents, would be conceived as either from self, from another, from both, or from no cause. And in every case it is untenable — thus having ascertained, he says:

children.text: na svato nāpi parato na dvābhyāṃ nāpyahetutaḥ |
children.translated_text: Not from self, not from another, not from both, not from no cause — /

children.text: utpannā jātu vidyante bhāvāḥ kvacana kecana || 3 ||
children.translated_text: there are no entities whatsoever, anywhere, that have ever arisen. // 3 //

body.text: tatra jātviti kadācidityarthaḥ | kvacanaśabda ādhāravacanaḥ kvacicchabdaparyāyaḥ kecanaśabda ādheyavacanaḥ kecicchabdaparyāyaḥ | tataścaivaṃ saṃbandhaḥ- naiva svata utpannā jātu vidyante bhāvāḥ, kvacana, kecana | evaṃ pratijñātrayamapi yojyam ||
body.translated_text: There, 'jātu' means 'at any time.' The word 'kvacana' expresses a locus and is synonymous with 'kvacit.' The word 'kecana' expresses a content and is synonymous with 'kecit.' Thus the connection is as follows: entities that have arisen from themselves simply do not exist, at any time, anywhere, any of them. In this way, the threefold proposition should also be construed.

body.text: nanu ca- naiva svata utpannā ityavadhāryamāṇe parata utpannā ityaniṣṭaṃ prāpnoti | na prāpnoti prasajyapratiṣedhasya vivakṣitatvāt, parato 'pyutpādasya pratiṣetsyamānatvāt | yayā copapattyā svata utpādo na saṃbhavati, sā-
body.translated_text: Now, if it is determined that 'they have not arisen from themselves,' the undesirable consequence would follow that they have arisen from another. [Reply:] It does not follow, because what is intended is a <s>prasajyapratiṣedha</s> (non-implicative negation), and because arising from another will also be negated. And the reasoning by which arising from self is impossible is to be ascertained through —

body.text:
tasmāddhi tasya bhavane na guṇo 'sti kaścij-
jātasya janma punareva ca naiva yuktam |
body.translated_text:
Therefore, in its existence there is no quality whatsoever;
and the birth of what has already been born is simply not reasonable. /

body.text: ityādinā madhyamakāvatārādidvāreṇāvaseyā ||
body.translated_text: — and so forth, through the gateway of the <s>Madhyamakāvatāra</s> and other [texts].

body.text: ācāryabuddhapālitastvāha- na svata utpadyante bhāvāḥ, tadutpādavaiyarthyāt, atiprasaṅgadoṣācca | na hi svātmanā vidyamānānāṃ padārthānāṃ punarutpāde prayojanamasti | atha sannapi jāyeta, na kadācinna jāyeta iti ||
body.translated_text: <s>Ācārya Buddhapālita</s>, for his part, says: 'Entities do not arise from themselves, because their arising would be pointless, and because of the fault of infinite regress. For there is no purpose in the re-arising of things that already exist by their own nature. And if something were to arise even though it [already] exists, it would never not arise.'

body.text: atraike dūṣaṇamāhuḥ- tadayuktam, hetudṛṣṭāntānabhidhānātparoktadoṣāparihārācca | prasaṅga vākyatvācca prakṛtārthaviparyayeṇa viparītārthasādhyataddharmavyaktau parasmādutpannābhāvājanmasāphalyāt janmaniro(bo?)dhācceti kṛtāntavirodhaḥ syāt ||
body.translated_text: Here, certain [critics] state the following objection: 'That is improper, because of the failure to state a reason (<s>hetu</s>) and an example (<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>), and because of the failure to refute the objections raised by the opponent. And because the statement is merely a <s>prasaṅga</s> (reductio) argument, by the reversal of the meaning of the subject, [one would] establish the opposite thesis — namely, that entities have arisen from another, that birth is fruitful, and that birth has an end — and thus there would be a contradiction with the established doctrine.'

body.text: sarvametaddūṣaṇamayujyamānaṃ vayaṃ paśyāmaḥ | kathaṃ kṛtvā? tatra yattāvaduktaṃ hetudṛṣṭāntānabhidhānāditi, tadayuktam | kiṃ kāraṇam? yasmātparaḥ svata utpattimabhyupagacchan, pṛcchayate- svata iti hetutvena tadeva cotpadyate iti? na ca vidyamānasya punarutpattau prayojanaṃ paśyāmaḥ, anavasthāṃ ca paśyāmaḥ | na ca tvayā utpannasya punarutpāda iṣyate 'navasthā cāpyaniṣṭeti | tasmānnirupapattika eva tvadvādaḥ svābhyupagamavirodhaśceti | kimiti codite paronābhyupaiti yato hetudṛṣṭāntopādānasāphalyaṃ syāt? atha svābhyupagamavirodhacodanayāpi paro na nivartate, tadā nirlajjatayā hetudṛṣṭāntābhyāmapi naiva nivarteta | na conmattakena sahāsmākaṃ vivāda iti | tasmātsarvathā priyānumānatāmevātmanaḥ ācāryaḥ prakaṭayati asthāne 'pyanumānaṃ praveśayan | na ca mādhyamikasya sataḥ svatantramanumānaṃ kartuṃ yuktaṃ pakṣāntarābhyupagamābhāvāt | tathoktamāryadevena-
body.translated_text: We see that all of this objection is unfounded. How so? First, as for the statement 'because of the failure to state a reason and an example' — that is improper. Why? Because the opponent who maintains arising from self is asked: 'By "from self," do you mean that that very same thing arises as a cause? And we see no purpose in the re-arising of something already existent, and we see an infinite regress. Nor do you accept the re-arising of what has already arisen, nor is infinite regress desired [by you]. Therefore your thesis is entirely without logical foundation and contradicts your own presupposition.' When this is pointed out, the opponent does not concede — so of what use would it be to adduce a reason and an example? If the opponent is not turned back even by pointing out the contradiction with his own presupposition, then, being shameless, he would not be turned back even by a reason and an example. And we do not debate with a madman. Therefore, in every way, the <s>Ācārya</s> [Bhāviveka] merely reveals his own fondness for inference, introducing inference even where it is out of place. Nor is it proper for a <s>Mādhyamika</s> to construct an independent inference, because of the absence of acceptance of any alternative thesis. As <s>Āryadeva</s> has said —

children.translated_text: He who has no thesis whatsoever —

neither 'existent,' nor 'non-existent,' nor 'both existent and non-existent' —
cannot be refuted even after a long time. //

body.text: vigrahavyāvartanyāṃ coktam-
body.translated_text: And in the <s>Vigrahavyāvartanī</s> it is said —

children.text: yadi kācana pratijñā syānme tata eva me bhaveddoṣaḥ |
children.translated_text: If I had any thesis, then indeed that fault would apply to me. /

children.text: nāsti ca mama pratijñā tasmānnaivāsti me doṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: But I have no thesis; therefore there is no fault in me. //
If I were to apprehend anything, I would either affirm or deny. /
Since those objects [apprehended through] perception and so forth do not exist for me, I am free from reproach. //

body.text: iti | yadā caivaṃ svatantrānumānānabhidhāyitvaṃ mādhyamikasya, tadā kutaḥ "nādhyātmikānyāyatanāni svata utpannāni" iti svatantrā pratijñā yasyāṃ sāṃkhyāḥ pratyavasthāpyante | ko 'rya pratijñārthaḥ kiṃ kāryātmakatvātsvata uta kāraṇātmakatvāditi | kiṃ cātaḥ? kāryātmakāccet siddha sādhanam, kāraṇātmakāccet viruddhārthatā, kāraṇātmanā vidyamānasyaiva sarvasyotpattimata utpādāditi | kuto 'smākaṃ vidyamānatvāditi heturyasya siddhasādhanaṃ viruddhārthatā vā syāt, yasya siddhasādhanasya yasyāśca viruddhārthatāyāḥ parihārārthaṃ yatnaṃ kariṣyāmaḥ | tasmātparoktadoṣāprasaṅgādeva tatparihāraḥ ācāryabuddhapālitena na varṇanīyaḥ ||
body.translated_text: And when the <s>Mādhyamika</s> thus does not employ independent inference, then where is the independent proposition 'the internal sense-bases have not arisen from themselves,' against which the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> would take a counter-position? What is the meaning of this proposition — is it because [the sense-bases] are of the nature of effect that they are 'from self,' or because they are of the nature of cause? And what follows? If because they are of the nature of effect, then the proof is redundant (<s>siddhasādhana</s>). If because they are of the nature of cause, then the meaning is contradictory — because everything that exists in the form of cause would arise, and thus arising would be from what already exists. Whence for us is there a reason 'because of existing' that would entail either the fault of redundant proof or contradictory meaning? And for whose redundant proof or whose contradictory meaning shall we exert ourselves in refutation? Therefore, since the faults stated by the opponent do not even arise, their refutation need not be elaborated by <s>Ācārya Buddhapālita</s>.

body.text: athāpi syāt- mādhyamikānāṃ pakṣahetudṛṣṭāntānāmasiddheḥ svatantrānumānānabhidhāyitvāt svata utpattipratiṣedhapratijñātārthasādhanaṃ mā bhūdubhayasiddhena vānumānena parapratijñānirākaraṇam | parapratijñāyāstu svata evānumānavirodhacodanayā svata eva pakṣahetudṛṣṭāntadoṣarahitaiḥ pakṣādibhirbhavitavyam | tataśca tadanabhidhānāt taddoṣāparihārācca sa eva doṣa iti | ucyate | naitadevam | kiṃ kāraṇam? yasmād yo hi yamarthaṃ pratijānīte, tena svaniścayavadanyeṣāṃ niścayotpādanecchayā yayā upapattyā asāvartho 'dhigataḥ saivopapattiḥ parasmai upadeṣṭavyā | tasmādeṣa tāvannyāyaḥ- yatpareṇaiva svābhyupagatapratijñātārthasādhanamupādeyam | na cāyaṃ (cānena?) paraṃ prati | hetudṛṣṭāntāsaṃbhavāt pratijñānusāratayaiva kevalaṃ svapratijñātārthasādhanamupādatta iti nirupapattikapakṣābhyupagamāt svātmānamevāyaṃ kevalaṃ visaṃvādayan na śaknoti pareṣāṃ niścayamādhātumiti | idamevāsya spaṣṭataraṃ dūṣaṇaṃ yaduta svapratijñātārthasādhanāsāmarthyamiti kimatrānumānabādhodbhāvanayā prayojanam? athāpyavaśyaṃ svato 'numānavirodhadoṣa udbhāvanīyaḥ, so 'pyudbhāvita evācāryabuddhapālitena | kathamiti cet, na svata utpadyante bhāvāḥ, tadutpādavaiyarthyāditi vacanāt, atra hi tadityanena svātmanā vidyamānasya parāmarśaḥ | kasmāditi cet, tathā hi tasya saṃgraheṇoktavākyasyaitadvivaraṇavākyam, na hi svātmanā vidyamānānāṃ punarutpāde prayojanamiti | anena ca vākyena sādhyasādhanadharmānugatasya paraprasiddhasya sādharmyadṛṣṭāntasyopādānam | tatra svātmanā vidyamānasyetyanena hetuparāmarśaḥ | utpādavayarthyādityanena sādhyadharmaparāmarśaḥ || tatra yathā- anityaḥ śabdaḥ kṛtakatvāt | kṛtakatvamanityaṃ
body.translated_text: But perhaps one might say: Since the <s>Mādhyamika</s>'s thesis, reason, and example are unestablished, and since he does not employ independent inference, let there be no proof of the proposition denying arising from self by means of an inference accepted by both parties, nor refutation of the opponent's thesis. But in the refutation of the opponent's thesis through the objection of inferential contradiction from the opponent's own [premises], the thesis, reason, and example must be free from defects from the opponent's own [standpoint]. And since these have not been stated, and since those defects have not been refuted, the same fault remains. [Reply:] We say: This is not so. Why? Because he who asserts a certain proposition, wishing to produce certainty in others just as he himself is certain, should teach to others the very reasoning by which he has ascertained that object. Therefore, this is the proper procedure: the opponent himself must adduce the proof of his own asserted proposition. And this [opponent] cannot [do so] with respect to [us]. Since a reason and an example are impossible, he has adduced the proof of his own asserted proposition merely in conformity with his thesis. Since he presupposes a thesis without logical foundation, merely deceiving himself, he is unable to produce certainty in others. This itself is the clearest refutation of him — namely, his inability to prove his own asserted proposition. What need, then, of bringing up inferential invalidation? But even if the fault of inferential contradiction from his own [premises] must necessarily be brought up, it has indeed already been brought up by <s>Ācārya Buddhapālita</s>. How? Because of the statement: 'Entities do not arise from themselves, because of the pointlessness of their arising.' Here, the word 'tat' (that) refers to what exists by its own nature. Why? Because the following is the explanatory statement of that summarized passage: 'For there is no purpose in the re-arising of things that exist by their own nature.' And by this statement, there is the employment of a <s>sādharmya</s> (concordant) example that is accepted by the opponent and that possesses the properties of the thing to be proved and the means of proof. Therein, 'what exists by its own nature' is the reference to the reason; 'pointlessness of arising' and so forth is the reference to the property to be proved. Just as — 'Sound is impermanent, because of being produced.

body.text: dṛṣṭaṃ yathā ghaṭaḥ | tathā ca kṛtakaḥ śabdaḥ | tasmātkṛtakatvādanitya iti kṛtakatvamatra upanayābhivyakto hetuḥ | evamihāpi- na svata utpadyante bhāvāḥ, svātmanā vidyamānānāṃ punarutpādavaiyarthyāt | iha hi svātmanā vidyamānaṃ puro 'vasthitaṃ ghaṭādikaṃ punarutpādānapekṣaṃ dṛṣṭam, tathā ca mṛtpiṇḍādyavasthāyāmapi yadi svātmanā vidyamānaṃ ghaṭādikamiti manyase, tadāpi tasya svātmanā vidyamānasya nāstyutpāda iti | evaṃ svātmanā vidyamānatvena upanayābhivyaktena punarutpādapratiṣedhāvyabhicāriṇā hetunā svata eva sāṃkhyasyānumānavirodhodbhāvanamanuṣṭhitameveti | tatkimucyate tadayuktaṃ hetudṛṣṭāntānabhidhānāditi?
body.translated_text: Being produced is seen to be impermanent, as in the case of a pot. And sound is produced. Therefore, because of being produced, it is impermanent' — here 'being produced' is the reason made explicit through the application. Even so here — 'Entities do not arise from themselves, because of the pointlessness of the re-arising of what exists by its own nature.' For here, a pot and so forth that exist by their own nature and stand before one are seen to require no re-arising. And if you think that even in the state of clay-lump and so forth, the pot and so forth exist by their own nature, then even so, for what exists by its own nature, there is no arising. Thus, by the reason made explicit through the application — namely, existing by one's own nature — the bringing up of inferential contradiction against the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> from his own [premises] has indeed been accomplished. So why is it said, 'That is improper, because of the failure to state a reason and an example'?

body.text: na ca kevalaṃ hetudṛṣṭāntānabhidhānaṃ na saṃbhavati, paroktadoṣāparihāradoṣo na saṃbhavati | kathaṃ kṛtvā? sāṃkhyā hi naiva abhivyaktarūpasya puro 'vasthitasya ghaṭasya punarabhivyaktimicchanti | tasyaiva ca iha dṛṣṭāntatvenopādānam, siddharūpatvāt | anabhivyaktarūpasya ca śaktirūpāpannasya utpattipratiṣedhaviśiṣṭasādhyatvāt kutaḥ siddhasādhanapakṣadoṣāśaṅkā, kuto vā hetorviruddhārthatāśaṅketi | tasmātsvato 'numānavirodhacodanāyāmapi yathopavarṇitadoṣābhāvātparoktadoṣāparihārāsaṃbhava eva | ityasaṃbaddhamevaitaddūṣaṇamiti vijñeyam ||
body.translated_text: Not only is the [alleged] failure to state a reason and example impossible, the fault of failure to refute the opponent's objections is also impossible. How so? For the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> do not at all desire the re-manifestation of a pot whose form is already manifest and stands before one. And it is precisely this that is employed here as the example, because it is of an established form. And since what is of unmanifest form, having assumed the form of a potentiality, is qualified as that whose arising is to be negated — the object to be proved — whence the suspicion of the thesis-defect of redundant proof, or whence the suspicion of the contradictory meaning of the reason? Therefore, even in the pointing out of inferential contradiction from his own [premises], since the faults described above do not exist, the impossibility of failure to refute the opponent's objections [is established]. Thus this objection should be understood as entirely incoherent.

body.text: ghaṭādikamityādiśabdena niravaśeṣotpitsupadārthasaṃgrahasya vivakṣitatvādanaikāntikatāpi paiṭādibhirnaiva saṃbhavati ||
body.translated_text: Since by the word 'etc.' in 'pots etc.,' the intention is to include all objects that are about to arise without remainder, the fault of inconclusiveness (<s>anaikāntikatā</s>) through [counter-examples such as] cloth and so forth is also entirely impossible.

body.text: athavā | ayamanyaḥ prayogamārgaḥ- puruṣavyatiriktāḥ padārthāḥ svata utpattivādinaḥ | tata eva na svata utpadyante | svātmanā vidyamānatvāt | puruṣavat | itīdamudāharaṇamudāhāryam ||
body.translated_text: Alternatively, here is another path of argument: 'Objects other than <s>Puruṣa</s> (the Self) do not arise from themselves, according to the proponent of arising from self. For that very reason, they do not arise from themselves — because of existing by their own nature — just like <s>Puruṣa</s>.' This should be stated as the illustrative example.

body.text: yadyapi ca abhivyaktivādina utpādapratiṣedho na bādhakaḥ, tathāpi abhivyaktāvutpādaśabdaṃ nipātya pūrvaṃ paścācca anupalabdhyupalabdhisādharmyeṇa utpādaśabdenābhivyakterevābhidhānādayaṃ pratiṣedho na abādhakaḥ ||
body.translated_text: And even though the negation of arising does not invalidate the proponent of manifestation (<s>abhivyakti</s>), nevertheless, by first applying the word 'arising' to manifestation, and then [showing that] through the concordance of non-apprehension before and apprehension after, the word 'arising' denotes manifestation itself — therefore this negation is not non-invalidating.

body.text: kathaṃ punarayaṃ yathoktārthābhidhānaṃ vinā vyastavicāro labhyata iti cet, taducyate | atha vākyāni kṛtāni, tāni mahārthatvādyathoditamarthaṃ saṃgṛhya pravṛttāni | tāni ca vyākhyāyamānāni yathoktamarthātmānaṃ prasūyanta iti nātra kiṃcidanupāttaṃ saṃbhāvyate ||
body.translated_text: But how, one may ask, is this detailed analysis obtained without the explicit statement of the meaning as described? To that we reply: The statements have been made; they proceed having gathered together the meaning as stated, because of their great import. And when those [statements] are being explained, they give rise to the meaning as stated — therefore nothing unincluded is to be suspected here.

body.text: prasaṅgaviparītena cārthena parasyaiva saṃbandho nāsmākam | svapratijñāyā abhāvāt | tataśca siddhāntavirodhāsaṃbhavaḥ | parasya ca yāvadbahavo doṣāḥ prasaṅgaviparītāpattyā āpadyante, tāvadasmābhirabhīṣyata eveti | kuto nu khalu aviparītācāryanāgārjunamatānusāriṇaḥ ācāryabuddhapālitasya sāvakāśavacanābhidhāyitvam, yato 'sya paro 'vakāśaṃ labheta? niḥsvabhāvabhāvavādinā sasvabhāvabhāvavādinaḥ prasaṅge āpa(pā?)dyamāne kutaḥ prasaṅgaviparītārthaprasaṅgitā? na hi śabdāḥ dāṇḍapāśikā iva vaktāramasvatantrayanti, kiṃ tarhi satyāṃ śaktau vakturvivakṣāmanuvidhīyante | tataśca (

children.translated_text: Pp_8

children.text: parapratijñāpratiṣedhamātraphalatvātprasaṅgāpādanasya nāsti prasaṅgaviparītārthāpattiḥ | tathā ca ācāryo bhūyasā prasaṅgāpattimukhenaiva parapakṣaṃ nirākaroti sma | tadyathā-
children.translated_text: since the bringing about of a <s>prasaṅga</s> has as its sole result the negation of the opponent's thesis, there is no consequence of the meaning obtained by reversal of the <s>prasaṅga</s>. And thus the <s>Ācārya</s> [<s>Nāgārjuna</s>] refuted the opponent's position overwhelmingly through the very method of <s>prasaṅga</s>-consequence. For example —

body.translated_text: And the connection with the meaning obtained by the reversal of the <s>prasaṅga</s> (reductio) belongs to the opponent alone, not to us, because of the non-existence of our own thesis. Therefore the impossibility of a contradiction with established doctrine [for us]. And as many faults as accrue to the opponent through the consequence of the reversal of the <s>prasaṅga</s> — all those are indeed desired by us. Whence indeed would there be room for objection in the statements of <s>Ācārya Buddhapālita</s>, who follows the unerring doctrine of <s>Ācārya Nāgārjuna</s>, such that the opponent could find an opening? When the proponent of entities having intrinsic nature is subjected to a reductio by the proponent of entities lacking intrinsic nature, how could there be the consequence of the reversal of the <s>prasaṅga</s>? For words do not render their speaker unfree, like prison-guards; rather, when there is capacity, they conform to the speaker's intention. Therefore, (

children.translated_text: Space does not exist at all prior to the defining characteristic of space. /

It would follow that it would be without a defining characteristic,
if it existed prior to the defining characteristic. //
When form is released from the cause of form, form without a cause would follow; /
but nothing whatsoever exists anywhere without a cause. //
An entity, to be sure, is not <s>nirvāṇa</s>, for it would bear the characteristic of old age and death; /

children.text: prasajyetāsti bhāvo hi na jarāmaraṇaṃ vinā ||
children.translated_text: it would follow that there is an entity without old age and death — but no entity exists without old age and death. //

body.text: ityādinā | atha arthavākyatvādācāryavākyānāṃ mahārthatve sati anekaprayoniṣpattihetutvaṃ parikalpyate, ācāryabuddhapālitavyākhyānānyapi kimiti na tathaiva parikalpyante?
body.translated_text: — and so forth. Now, if because the <s>Ācārya</s>'s statements are meaningful, it is conceived that they, being of great import, are the cause of the production of multiple lines of argument, why then are <s>Ācārya Buddhapālita</s>'s explanations not likewise conceived?

body.text: atha syāt- vṛttikārāṇāmeṣa nyāyaḥ, yatprayogavākyavistarābhidhānaṃ kartavyamiti, etadapi nāsti, vigrahavyāvartanyā vṛttiṃ kurvatāpyācāryeṇa prayogavākyānabhidhānāt ||
body.translated_text: If one were to say that this is the proper method for commentators — that the detailed statement of argument-formulations must be made — even this is not so, because even the <s>Ācārya</s> [<s>Nāgārjuna</s>], when composing the commentary on the <s>Vigrahavyāvartanī</s>, did not employ detailed argument-formulations.

body.text: api ca | ātmanastarkaśāstrātikauśalamātramāviścikīrṣayā aṅgīkṛtamadhyamakadarśanasyāpi yatsvatantraprayogavākyābhidhānaṃ tadatitarāmanekadoṣasamudāyāspadamasya tārkikasyopalakṣyate | kathaṃ kṛtvā? tatra yattāvadevamuktam- atra prayogavākyaṃ bhavati- na paramārthataḥ ādhyātmikānyāyatanāni svata utpannāni, vidyamānatvāt, caitanyavaditi | kimartha punaratra paramārthata iti viśeṣaṇamupādīyate? lokasaṃvṛtyābhyupagatasya utpādasya apratiṣidhyamānatvāt, pratiṣedhe ca abhyupetabādhāprasaṅgāditi cet, naitadyuktam | saṃvṛtyāpi svata utpattyanabhyupagamāt | yathoktaṃ sūtre-
body.translated_text: Moreover, the statement of an independent proof-formula (<s>svatantraprayogavākya</s>) by one who has accepted the <s>Madhyamaka</s> view merely out of a desire to display his own excessive skill in the science of logic — this is observed to be the locus of a multitude of extremely numerous faults in the case of this logician. How so? To begin with, as he has stated: 'Here the proof-formula is: The inner sense-bases (<s>āyatana</s>) are not, in the ultimate sense (<s>paramārthataḥ</s>), produced from themselves, because they exist (<s>vidyamānatvāt</s>), like consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>).' Now, for what purpose is the qualifier 'in the ultimate sense' employed here? If it is said that this is because the arising admitted in worldly convention (<s>lokasaṃvṛti</s>) is not being negated, and because negating it would entail the fault of contradicting what is accepted — this is not correct. Because even in convention (<s>saṃvṛti</s>), arising from self is not accepted. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>:

body.text: "sa cāyaṃ bījahetuko 'ṅkura utpadyamāno na svayaṃkṛto na parakṛto nobhayakṛto nāpyahetusamutpanno niśvarakālāṇuprakṛtisvabhāvasaṃbhūtaḥ" iti |
body.translated_text: "This sprout, arising from the seed as its cause, is neither self-made (<s>svayaṃkṛta</s>), nor other-made (<s>parakṛta</s>), nor made by both, nor arisen without a cause; it is not produced from God (<s>Īśvara</s>), time (<s>kāla</s>), atoms (<s>aṇu</s>), or primordial nature (<s>Prakṛti</s>), nor from its own inherent nature (<s>svabhāva</s>)."

body.text: tathā-
body.translated_text: Likewise:

children.text: bījasya sato yathāṅkuro na ca yo bīju sa caiva aṅkuro |
children.translated_text: Just as the sprout exists when the seed exists, yet that which is the seed is not itself the sprout, /

children.text: na ca anyu tato na caiva tadevamanucchedaaśāśvatadharmatā ||
children.translated_text: nor is it other than the seed — thus the nature of <s>dharmas</s> is neither annihilation (<s>uccheda</s>) nor permanence (<s>śāśvata</s>). //

body.text: ihāpi vakṣyati-
body.translated_text: Here too [in our text] it will be stated:

children.text: pratītya yadyadbhavati na hi tāvattadeva tat |
children.translated_text: Whatever arises dependently (<s>pratītya</s>) — that is indeed not identical with that [upon which it depends]. /
Nor is it other than that; therefore it is neither annihilated nor permanent. //

body.text: iti ||
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: paramatāpekṣaṃ viśeṣaṇamiti cet, tadayuktam | saṃvṛtyāpi tadīyavyavasthānabhyupagamāt | satyadvayāviparītadarśanaparibhraṣṭā eva hi tīrthikā yāvadubhayathāpi niṣidhyante tāvad guṇa eva saṃbhāvyata iti | evaṃ paramatāpekṣamapi viśeṣaṇābhidhānaṃ na yujyate ||
body.translated_text: If it is said that the qualifier is with reference to the opponent's position — that too is incorrect. Because even in convention (<s>saṃvṛti</s>), the establishment of that [opponent's position] is not accepted. For the <s>tīrthikas</s> (non-Buddhist philosophers), having fallen from the correct understanding of the two truths (<s>satyadvaya</s>), are indeed to be refuted on both counts — and therein lies the benefit. Thus, even stating a qualifier with reference to the opponent's position is not appropriate.

body.text: na cāpi lokaḥ svatautpattiṃ pratipannaḥ, yatastadapekṣayāpi viśeṣaṇasāphalyaṃ syāt | loko hi svataḥ parata ityevamādikaṃ vicāramanavatārya kāraṇātkāryamutpadyate ityetāvanmātraṃ pratipannaḥ | evamācāryo 'pi vyavasthāpayāmāsa | iti sarvathā viśeṣaṇavaiphalyameva niścīyate ||
body.translated_text: Nor has the ordinary world (<s>loka</s>) accepted arising from self, such that the qualifier would serve a purpose with reference to that. For the world, without entering into analysis such as 'from self,' 'from other,' and so forth, simply accepts that an effect arises from a cause — nothing more than this. The Master (<s>Ācārya</s>) too has established it thus. Therefore, in every case, the futility of the qualifier is conclusively determined.

body.text: api ca | yadi saṃvṛtyā utpattipratiṣedhanirācikīrṣuṇā viśeṣaṇametadupādīyate, tadā svato 'siddhādhāre pakṣadoṣaḥ, āśrayāsiddhau vā hetudoṣaḥ syāt | paramārthataḥ svataścakṣurādyāyatanānāmanabhyupagamāt | saṃvṛtyā cakṣurādisadbhāvādadoṣa iti cet, paramārthata ityetattarhi kasya viśeṣaṇam? sāṃvṛtānāṃ cakṣurādīnāṃ paramārthata utpattipratiṣedhād utpattipratiṣedhaviśeṣaṇe paramārthagrahaṇamiti cet, evaṃ tarhi evameva vaktavyaṃ syāt- sāṃvṛtānāṃ cakṣurādīnāṃ paramārthato nāstyutpattiriti | na caivamucyate | ucyamāne 'pi parairvastusatāmeva cakṣurādīnāmabhyupagamāt, prajñaptisatāmanabhyupagamāt parato 'siddhādhāraḥ pakṣadoṣaḥ syāditi na yuktametat ||
body.translated_text: Moreover, if this qualifier is adopted by one who does not wish to negate arising in convention (<s>saṃvṛti</s>), then there would be the defect in the thesis (<s>pakṣadoṣa</s>) of an unestablished basis (<s>asiddhādhāra</s>), or the defect in the reason (<s>hetudoṣa</s>) of an unestablished substratum (<s>āśrayāsiddhi</s>). Because, in the ultimate sense, the sense-bases such as the eye and so on are not accepted as arising from themselves. If it is said that in convention, because of the real existence of the eye and so on, there is no defect — then the qualifier 'in the ultimate sense' is a qualifier of what? If it is said that the qualifier 'ultimate' applies to the negation of arising, since there is a negation in the ultimate sense of the arising of the conventionally posited eye and so on — then one should simply state: 'The arising of the conventionally posited eye and so on does not exist in the ultimate sense.' But this is not what is said. Moreover, even if it were said thus, since the opponents accept the eye and so on as real entities (<s>vastusatā</s>) and do not accept them as merely nominal entities (<s>prajñaptisatā</s>), there would be the defect in the thesis of an unestablished basis from the opponent's perspective. Therefore this is not correct.

body.text: atha syāt- yathā anityaḥ śabda iti dharmadharmisāmānyameva gṛhyate na viśeṣaḥ, viśeṣagrahaṇe hi sati anumānānumeyavyavahārābhāvaḥ syāt | tathā hi- yadi cāturmahābhautikaḥ śabdo gṛhyate, sa parasyāsiddhaḥ | athākāśaguṇo gṛhyate, sa bauddhasya svato 'siddhaḥ | tathā vaiśeṣikasya śabdānityatāṃ pratijānānasya yadi kāryaḥ śabdo gṛhyate, sa parato 'siddhaḥ | atha vyaṅgayaḥ, sa svato 'siddhaḥ | evaṃ yathāsaṃbhavaṃ vināśo 'pi yadi sahetukaḥ, sa bauddhasya svato 'siddhaḥ | atha nirhetukaḥ, sa parasyāsiddha iti | tasmād yathātra dharmadharmisāmānyamātrameva gṛhyate, evamihāpi dharmimātramutsṛṣṭaviśeṣaṇaṃ grahīṣyata iti cet, naitadevam | yasmād yadaivotpādapratiṣedho 'tra sādhyadharmo 'bhipretaḥ, tadaiva dharmiṇastadādhārasya viparyāsamātrāsāditātmabhāvasya pracyutiḥ svayamevānenāṅgīkṛtā | bhinnau hi viparyāsāviparyāsau | tadyadā viparyāsena asatsattvena gṛhyate, taimirikeṇeva keśādi, tadā kutaḥ sadbhūtapadārthaleśasyāpyupalabdhiḥ? yadā ca aviparyāsādabhūtaṃ nādhyāropitaṃ vitaimirikeṇeva keśādi, tadā kuto 'sadbhūtapadārthaleśasyāpyupalabdhiḥ, yena tadānīṃ saṃvṛtiḥ syāt? ata evoktamācāryapādaiḥ-
body.translated_text: Now, one might say: Just as in 'Sound is impermanent,' only the generality of the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>) and the property (<s>dharma</s>) is grasped, not the specific [kind], since if specifics were grasped, the practice of inference and what is to be inferred would be rendered impossible — for instance, if sound as composed of the four great elements is grasped, it is unestablished for the opponent; if grasped as a quality of space, it is unestablished for the Buddhist himself; similarly, for the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> asserting the impermanence of sound, if sound as an effect is grasped, it is unestablished for the opponent; if as a manifestation (<s>vyaṅgya</s>), it is unestablished for himself; likewise, destruction too, if it has a cause, is unestablished for the Buddhist himself; if causeless, it is unestablished for the opponent — therefore, just as there only the generality of the property-bearer and the property is grasped, so too here only the bare property-bearer without specific qualification will be grasped. This is not so. Because the very moment the negation of arising is intended as the property to be proved (<s>sādhyadharma</s>), the property-bearer — that which serves as its basis, whose existence is established only by error — undergoes dissolution by his own admission. For error and non-error are distinct. When through error what does not exist is grasped as existing — just as hair and the like by one with a visual disorder (<s>taimirika</s>) — then how can there be even a trace of apprehension of a real entity? And when through non-error what does not exist is not superimposed — just as hair and the like by one without a visual disorder — then how can there be even a trace of apprehension of an unreal entity, by which convention (<s>saṃvṛti</s>) would obtain? Therefore the Master (<s>Ācāryapāda</s>) has stated:

children.translated_text: If I had any thesis whatsoever, then that fault would attach to me. /
But I have no thesis at all; therefore I am without fault. //

body.text: yataścaivaṃ bhinnau viparyāsāviparyāsau, ato viduṣāmaviparītāvasthāyāṃ viparītasyāsaṃbhavātkutaḥ sāṃvṛtaṃ cakṣuḥ yasya dharmitvaṃ syāt? iti na vyāvartate 'siddhādhāre pakṣadoṣaḥ, āśrayāsiddho vā hetudoṣaḥ | ityaparihāra evāyam ||
body.translated_text: And since error and non-error are thus distinct, because in the non-erroneous state of the wise the erroneous does not obtain, where would there be a conventional eye to serve as the property-bearer? Thus the defect in the thesis of an unestablished basis, or the defect in the reason of an unestablished substratum, is not avoided. And this remains without remedy.

body.text: nidarśanasyāpi nāsti sāmyam | tatra hi śabdasāmānyamanityatāsāmānyaṃ ca avivakṣitaviśeṣaṃ dvayorapi saṃvidyate | na tvevaṃ cakṣuḥ sāmānyaṃ śūnyatāśūnyatāvādibhyāṃ saṃvṛtyā aṅgīkṛtaṃ nāpi paramārthataḥ | iti nāsti nidarśanasya sāmyam ||
body.translated_text: The example too lacks similarity. For there, the generality of sound and the generality of impermanence, without specifying any particular [nature], are accepted by both. But the generality of the eye is not accepted in convention by both the proponents of emptiness and non-emptiness, nor in the ultimate sense. Thus there is no similarity in the example.

body.text: yaścāyamasiddhādhārapakṣadoṣodbhāvane vidhiḥ, eṣa eva sattvādityasya hetorasiddhārthatodbhāvane 'pi yojyaḥ ||
body.translated_text: And the very method used to show the defect of the thesis having an unestablished basis — this same method should be applied to show the unestablished meaning of the reason 'because it exists' (<s>sattvāt</s>).

body.text: itthaṃ caitadevam, yatsvayamaṣyanenāyaṃ yathokto 'rtho 'bhyupagatastārkikeṇa | santyevādhyātmikāyatanotpādakā hetvādayaḥ, tathā tathāgatena nirdeśāt | yaddhi yathā tathāgatenāsti nirdiṣṭaṃ tattathā, tadyathā śāntaṃ nirvāṇamiti ||
body.translated_text: Furthermore, it is precisely thus — for even this logician himself has accepted the meaning stated as follows. 'There do indeed exist causes and such conditions (<s>hetvādi</s>) that produce the inner sense-bases (<s>āyatana</s>), because they have been so indicated by the <s>Tathāgata</s>. For whatever has been indicated as existing by the <s>Tathāgata</s> is so — for example, "<s>Nirvāṇa</s> is peace."'

body.text: asya paropakṣiptasya sādhanasyedaṃ dūṣaṇamabhihitamanena- ko hi bhavatāmabhipreto 'tra hetvarthaḥ? saṃvṛtyā tathā tathāgatena nirdeśāt, uta paramārthata iti? saṃvṛtyā cet, svato hetorasiddhārthatā | paramārthataścet,
body.translated_text: To this proof adduced by the opponent, the following refutation has been stated by him [<s>Candrakīrti</s>]: 'What is the meaning of the reason intended by you here? Is it that in convention (<s>saṃvṛti</s>) the <s>Tathāgata</s> has so indicated, or in the ultimate sense (<s>paramārthataḥ</s>)? If in convention, the reason has an unestablished meaning from one's own standpoint. And if in the ultimate sense —

body.text: na sannāsanna sadasaddharmo nirvartate yadā |
body.translated_text: Since neither an existent, nor a non-existent, nor an existent-and-non-existent <s>dharma</s> is produced, /

body.text: sadasadubhayātmakakāryapratyayatvanirākaraṇāt, tadā-
body.translated_text: because the production from a cause-and-condition of the nature of existent, non-existent, or both is negated — at that time,

body.text: kathaṃ nirvartako heturevaṃ sati hi yujyate ||
body.translated_text: how can a producing cause be appropriate in these circumstances? //

body.text: naivāsau nirvartako heturiti vākyārthaḥ | tataśca paramārthato nirvartyanirvartakatvāsiddheḥ asiddhārthatā viruddhārthatā vā hetoriti ||
body.translated_text: That is to say: that is certainly not a producing cause — this is the meaning of the statement. And hence, since the production and producer relationship is unestablished in the ultimate sense, the reason has an unestablished meaning or a contradictory meaning.'

body.text: yataścaivaṃ svayamevāmunā nyāyena hetorasiddhiraṅgīkṛtānena, tasmātsarveṣvevānumāneṣu vastu dharmopanyastahetukeṣu svata evaṃ hetvādīnāmasiddhatvāt sarvāṇyeva sādhanāni vyāhanyante | tadyathā- na paramārthataḥ parebhyastatpratyayebhyaḥ ādhyātmikāyatanajanma, paratvāt, tadyathā paṭasya | athavā- na pare paramārthena vivakṣitāḥ cakṣurādyādhyātmikāyatananirvartakāḥ pratyayā iti pratīyante, paratvāt, tadyathā tantvādaya iti | paratvādikamatra svata evāsiddham ||
body.translated_text: And since he has thus himself, by this very reasoning, accepted the unestablished nature of the reason, therefore in all inferences whatsoever that employ a reason bearing upon real properties of a thing, because causes and such are themselves unestablished in precisely this way, all proofs are vitiated. For instance: 'In the ultimate sense, the inner sense-bases do not have their birth from others, i.e., from their respective conditions, because [those conditions are] other, just like a cloth.' Or alternatively: 'Others, i.e., the conditions that are intended as producers of the inner sense-bases such as the eye, are not understood in the ultimate sense to be producers, because they are other, just like threads and so on.' Here, the otherness and so on is itself unestablished from one's own standpoint.

body.text: yathā cānena- utpannā eva ādhyātmikā bhāvāḥ, tadviṣayiviśiṣṭavyavahārakaraṇāt- ityasya parābhihitasya hetorasiddhārthatāmudbhāvayiṣuṇā idamuktam, atha samāhitasya yoginaḥ prajñācakṣuṣā bhāvayāthātmyaṃ paśyataḥ utpādagatyādayaḥ santi paramārthata iti sādhyate, tadā tadviṣayiviśiṣṭavyavahārakaraṇāditi hetorasiddhārthatā, gaterapyutpādaniṣedhādeva niṣedhāditi | evaṃ svakṛtasādhane 'pi paramārthato 'gataṃ naiva gamyate, adhvatvāt, gatādhvavaditi adhvatvahetoḥ svata evāsiddhārthatā yojyā ||
body.translated_text: And when he — wishing to show the unestablished meaning of the opponent's reason stated as: 'The inner entities have indeed arisen, because they occasion the distinctive ordinary usage pertaining to their respective objects' — said: 'Then, if it is being proved that for a meditator in <s>samādhi</s>, who with the eye of wisdom (<s>prajñācakṣus</s>) sees the true nature of entities, arising, going, and so forth exist in the ultimate sense, then the reason "because they occasion the distinctive ordinary usage pertaining to their respective objects" has an unestablished meaning, since going too is negated by the very negation of arising.' Even so, in his own proof too — 'In the ultimate sense, what has not gone is indeed not being gone to, because it is a path (<s>adhvan</s>), like the path already gone' — the unestablished meaning of the reason 'because it is a path' from one's own standpoint should be applied.

body.text: na paramārthataḥ sabhāgaṃ cakṣū rūpaṃ paśyati, cakṣurindriyatvāt, tadyathā tatsabhāgam | tathā- na cakṣuḥ prekṣate rūpam, bhautikatvāt, rūpavat | kharasvabhāvā na mahī, bhūtatvāt, tadyathānirlaḥ, ityādiṣu hetvādyasiddhiḥ svata eva yojyā ||
body.translated_text: 'The similar eye (<s>sabhāga</s>) does not, in the ultimate sense, see form, because it is the eye-faculty, like the dissimilar [eye].' Likewise: 'The eye does not perceive form, because it is elemental (<s>bhautika</s>), like form.' 'The earth is not hard by nature, because it is an element (<s>bhūta</s>), like water.' In these and similar cases, the unestablished nature of the reason and so forth from one's own standpoint should be applied.

body.text: sattvāditi cāyaṃ hetuḥ parato 'naikāntikaḥ | kiṃ sattvāt caitanyavannādhyātmikānyāyatanāni svata utpadyantām, utāho ghaṭādivat svata utpadyantāmiti ghaṭādīnāṃ sādhyasamatvānnānaikāntikateti cet, naitadevam, tathānabhidhānāt ||
body.translated_text: And this reason 'because it exists' (<s>sattvāt</s>) is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) from the opponent's standpoint. Whether the inner sense-bases should not arise from themselves because they exist, like consciousness; or whether they should arise from themselves because they exist, like a pot and the like — since pots and the like are on an equal footing with what is to be proved (<s>sādhyasama</s>), there is no inconclusiveness. This is not correct [to say], because it is not stated in that way.

body.text: nanu ca yathā parakīyeṣvanumāneṣu dūṣaṇamuktam, evaṃ svānumāneṣvapi yathoktadūṣaṇaprasaṅge sati sa eva asiddhādhārāsiddhahetvādidoṣaḥ prāpnoti, tataśca yaḥ ubhayordoṣaḥ, na tenaikaścodyo bhavatīti sarvametaddūṣaṇamayuktaṃ jāyata iti | ucyate | svatantramanumānaṃ bruvatāmayaṃ doṣo jāyate | na vayaṃ svatantramanumānaṃ prayuñjmamahe parapratijñāniṣedhaphalatvādasmadanumānānām | tathā hi- paraḥ cakṣuḥ paśyatīti pratipannaḥ | sa tatprasiddhenaivānumānena nirākriyate- cakṣuṣaḥ svātmādarśanadharmamicchasi, paradarśanadharmāvinābhāvitvaṃ cāṅgīkṛtam, tasmād yatra yatra svātmādarśanaṃ tatra tatra paradarśanamapi nāsti, tadyathā ghaṭe, asti ca cakṣuṣaḥ svātmādarśanam, tasmāt paradarśanamapyasya naivāsti | tataśca svātmādarśanaviruddhaṃ nīlādiparadarśanaṃ svaprasiddhenaivānumānena virudhyata iti etāvanmātramasmadanūmānairudbhāvyata iti kuto 'smatpakṣe yathoktadoṣāvatāraḥ, yataḥ samānadoṣatā syāt?
body.translated_text: Now, it may be objected: 'Just as the refutation has been stated against the opponent's inferences, so too in one's own inferences the same refutation as stated would apply — the very same defects of unestablished basis, unestablished reason, and so forth would obtain. And therefore whatever fault belongs to both parties cannot be charged against one alone — hence all this refutation turns out to be inappropriate.' The reply is: This fault applies to those who formulate an independent inference (<s>svatantra anumāna</s>). We do not employ an independent inference, because the result of our inferences is solely the negation of the opponent's thesis. For instance: the opponent holds that the eye sees. He is refuted by an inference established precisely on his own terms: 'You accept that the eye has the property of not seeing itself, and you also accept the inseparability of seeing what is other [from self-seeing]. Therefore, wherever there is non-seeing of self, there too seeing of other does not exist — just as with a pot. And the eye does have non-seeing of itself. Therefore, seeing of other too does not belong to it.' Thus, the seeing of other — blue and so on — which contradicts non-self-seeing, is refuted by an inference established precisely on his own terms. Only this much is brought out by our inferences. So where is the entry of the stated defects into our position, on account of which there would be an equality of fault?

body.text: kiṃ punaḥ- anyataraprasiddhenāpyanumānenāstyanumānabādhā | asti, sā ca svaprasiddhenaiva hetunā, na paraprasiddhena, lokata evaṃ dṛṣṭatvāt | kadāciddhi loke arthipratyarthibhyāṃ pramāṇīkṛtasya sākṣiṇo vacanena jayo bhavati parājayo vā, kadācit svavacanena | paravacanena tu na jayo nāpi parājayaḥ | yathā ca loke, tathā nyāye 'pi | laukikasyaiva vyavahārasya nyāyaśāstre prastutatvāt | ata eva kaiściduktam- na parataḥ prasiddhibalādanumānabādhā, paraprasiddhereva nirācikīrṣitatvāditi | yastu manyate- ya eva ubhayaniścitavādī, sa pramāṇaṃ dūṣaṇaṃ vā, nānyataraprasiddhasaṃdigdhavācī iti, tenāpi laukikīṃ vyavasthāmanurudhyamānena anumāne yathokta eva nyāyo 'bhyupeyaḥ ||
body.translated_text: But is there not refutation by inference even through what is established for only one party? There is — and that too through a reason established on one's own terms, not through one established on the other's terms, since this is how it is seen in the world. For sometimes in the world, when a witness has been accepted as authoritative by both parties — the plaintiff and the defendant — victory or defeat occurs through his statement; sometimes through one's own statement. But through the other party's statement, there is neither victory nor defeat. Just as in the world, so too in logic — because it is ordinary worldly practice itself that is elaborated in the science of logic. Therefore some have said: 'There is no refutation by inference on the strength of what is established for the other party, since what is established for the other party is precisely what one seeks to refute.' And even one who holds that 'only one whose statements are certain for both parties is authoritative as proof or refutation, not one whose statements are uncertain or established for only one party' — even he, following worldly convention, must accept precisely the principle stated above regarding inference.

body.text: tathā hi nobhayaprasiddhena vā āgamena bādhā, kiṃ tarhi svaprasiddhenāpi ||
body.translated_text: Accordingly, there is no refutation even by a scripture (<s>āgama</s>) established for both parties — rather, [it is] even by one established for oneself alone.

body.text: svārthānumāne tu sarvatra svaprasiddhireva garīyasī, nobhayaprasiddhiḥ | ata eva tarkalakṣaṇābhidhānaṃ niṣprayojanam, yathāsvaprasiddhayā upapattyā buddhaistadanabhijñavineyajanānugrahāt | ityalaṃ prasaṅgena | prakṛtameva vyākhyāsyāmaḥ ||
body.translated_text: In inference for oneself (<s>svārthānumāna</s>), moreover, what is established for oneself alone is in every case paramount, not what is established for both. Therefore, stating the definition of logic (<s>tarkalakṣaṇa</s>) is purposeless — since the <s>Buddhas</s>, through reasoning established for themselves, [teach] out of compassion for those to be guided who are unfamiliar with it. But enough of this digression. We shall explain the main topic itself.

body.text: parato 'pi notpadyante bhāvāḥ | parābhāvādeva etacca-
body.translated_text: Entities do not arise from other (<s>parata</s>) either. Because of the very non-existence of 'other' (<s>parābhāvāt</s>). And this —

body.text: na hi svabhāvo bhāvānāṃ pratyayādiṣu vidyate |
body.translated_text: For the intrinsic nature (<s>svabhāva</s>) of entities is not found in conditions and so forth —

body.text: ityatra pratipādayiṣyati | tataśca parābhāvādeva nāpi parata utpadyante | api ca-
body.translated_text: this he will demonstrate here. And therefore, since there is precisely the non-existence of the other, they do not arise from another either. Moreover —

body.text:
anyatpratītya yadi nāma paro 'bhaviṣya-
jjāyeta tarhi bahulaḥ śikhino 'ndhakāraḥ |
body.translated_text: If that which arises in dependence on another were indeed 'other,' then abundant darkness would arise from flames;

body.text:
sarvasya janma ca bhavetkhalu sarvataśca
tulyaṃ paratvamakhile 'janake 'pi yasmāt ||
body.translated_text: and the arising of everything from everything would follow, since otherness is equal in all things, even in what is not a cause. //

body.text: ityādinā [madhyamakāvatārāt] parata utpattipratiṣedho 'vaseyaḥ ||
body.translated_text: By such [verses from the <s>Madhyamakāvatāra</s>], the refutation of arising from another should be understood.

body.text: ācāryabuddhapālitastu vyācaṣṭe- na parata utpadyante bhāvāḥ, sarvataḥ sarvasaṃbhavaprasaṅgāt ācāryabhāvaviveko dūṣaṇamāha- tadatra prasaṅgavākyatvāt sādhyasādhanaviparyayaṃ kṛtvā, svataḥ ubhayataḥ ahetuto vā utpadyante bhāvāḥ, kutaścitkasyacidutpatteḥ, iti prākpakṣavirodhaḥ | anyathā sarvataḥ sarvasaṃbhavaprasaṅgāt ityasya sādhanadūṣaṇānantaḥpātitvādasaṃgatārthametat [iti] | etadapyasaṃgatārtham | pūrvameva pratipāditatvād dūṣaṇāntaḥpātitvācca parapratijñātārthadūṣaṇeneti yatkiṃcidetaditi na punaryatna āsthīyate ||
body.translated_text: <s>Ācārya Buddhapālita</s> explains: 'Entities do not arise from another, because of the absurd consequence that everything would arise from everything.' <s>Ācārya Bhāvaviveka</s> states a fault: 'Since this is a statement of absurd consequence (<s>prasaṅga</s>), by reversing the thesis and the proof — [one could argue:] entities arise from themselves, from both, or from no cause, since some particular thing arises from some particular thing at some particular time — this contradicts the opponent's position. Otherwise, the statement "because of the absurd consequence that everything would arise from everything" would fall within the scope of the proof's own fault, and the meaning would be incoherent.' This [objection] too is incoherent. Since it has already been demonstrated previously, and since [the objection itself] falls within the scope of the fault, refutation of the thesis asserted by the opponent [suffices] — hence no further effort is applied to this trivial matter.

body.text: dvābhyāmapi nopajāyante bhāvāḥ, ubhayapakṣābhihitadoṣaprasaṅgāt pratyekamutpādāsāmarthyācca | vakṣyati hi-
body.translated_text: Entities do not arise from both either, because of the absurd consequence of the faults stated in each of the two positions, and because of the incapacity for arising from each individually. For he will say —

body.text: syādubhābhyāṃ kṛtaṃ duḥkhaṃ syādekaikakṛtaṃ yadi | iti ||
body.translated_text: 'Suffering would be made by both, if it were made by each of the two.' //

body.text: ahetuto 'pi notpadyante-
body.translated_text: Nor do they arise from no cause —

body.text: hetāvasati kāryaṃ ca kāraṇaṃ ca na vidyate |
body.translated_text: 'When there is no cause, neither effect nor cause is found.' //

body.text: iti vakṣyamāṇadoṣaprasaṅgāt,
body.translated_text: Because of the absurd consequence of the fault to be stated, and

body.text:
gṛhyeta naiva ca jagadyadi hetuśūnyaṃ
syādyadvadeva gaganotpalavarṇagandhau ||
body.translated_text: 'If the world were devoid of causes, it would never be apprehended — just as the color and fragrance of a sky-flower [are not apprehended].' //

body.text: ityādidoṣaprasaṅgācca ||
body.translated_text: Because of the absurd consequence of such faults as these.

body.text: ācāryabuddhapālitastvāha- ahetuto notpadyante bhāvāḥ, sadā ca sarvataśca sarvasaṃbhavaprasaṅgāt | atrācāryabhāvaviveko dūṣaṇamāha- atrāpi prasaṅgavākyatvāt yadi viparītasādhyasādhanavyaktivākyārtha iṣyate, tadā etaduktaṃ bhavati- hetuta utpadyante bhāvāḥ, kadācit kutaścit kasyacidutpatteḥ, ārambhasāphalyācca | seyaṃ vyākhyā na yuktā prāguktadoṣāditi | tadetadayuktam, pūrvoditaparihārādityapare ||
body.translated_text: <s>Ācārya Buddhapālita</s> states: 'Entities do not arise from no cause, because of the absurd consequence that everything would arise always and from everything.' Here <s>Ācārya Bhāvaviveka</s> states a fault: 'Here too, since this is a statement of absurd consequence, if the meaning of the statement is desired as the expression of the reversed thesis and proof, then this amounts to saying: entities arise from a cause, since some particular thing arises from some particular thing at some particular time, and since effort has its fruit. This explanation is not correct, because of the fault stated earlier.' That [objection] is incorrect, because of the refutation already given above — so say others.

body.text: yaccāpi īśvarādīnāmupasaṃgrahārtham, tadāpi na yuktam | īśvarādīnāṃ svaparobhayapakṣeṣu yathābhyupagamamantarbhāvāditi ||
body.translated_text: As for the [claim] that [the absurd consequence argument] is for the purpose of including [the views of] <s>Īśvara</s> and others — that too is not correct, since [the views of] <s>Īśvara</s> and others are subsumed within the positions of self, other, and both, according to their respective tenets.

body.text: tasmāt prasādhitametannāstyutpāda iti | utpādāsaṃbhavācca siddho 'nutpādādiviśiṣṭa pratītyasamutpāda iti ||
body.translated_text: Therefore it is established that there is no arising. And since arising is impossible, <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> (dependent origination), characterized by non-arising and so forth, is established.

children.text: atrāha- yadyevamanutpādādiviśiṣṭaḥ pratītyasamutpādo vyavasthito bhavadbhiḥ, yattarhi bhagavatoktam- avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārā avidyānirodhātsaṃskāranirodha iti, tathā-
children.translated_text: Here one objects: If <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>, characterized by non-arising and so forth, is thus established by you, then what about the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s statement: 'Conditioned by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) are <s>saṃskāras</s> (formations); from the cessation of <s>avidyā</s> comes the cessation of <s>saṃskāras</s>'? And also —
'Impermanent, alas, are those <s>saṃskāras</s> (formations), subject to arising and passing away;

children.text: utpadya hi nirudhyante teṣāṃ vyupaśamaḥ sukhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: having arisen, they cease — their quiescence is bliss.' //

body.text: tathā- utpādādvā tathāgatānāmanutpādādvā tathāgatānāṃ sthitaivaiṣā dharmāṇāṃ dharmatā, eko dharmaḥ sattvasthitaye yaduta catvāra āhārāḥ, dvau dharmau lokaṃ pālayato hrīścāpatrāpyaṃ cetyādi, tathā- paralokādihāgamanamihalokācca paralokagamanamiti, evaṃ nirodhādiviśiṣṭaḥ pratītyasamutpādo deśito bhagavatā, sa kathaṃ na ni (vi?) rudhyata iti? yata evaṃ nirodhādayaḥ pratītyasamutpādasyopalabhyante, ata evedaṃ madhyamakaśāstraṃ praṇītamācāryeṇa neyanītārthasūtrāntavibhāgopadarśanārtham | tatra ya ete pratītyasamutpādasyotpādādaya uktāḥ, na te vigatāvidyātimirānāsravaviṣayasvabhāvāpekṣayā, kiṃ tarhi avidyātimiropahatamatinayanajñānaviṣayāpekṣayā ||
body.translated_text: And also: 'Whether <s>Tathāgatas</s> arise or whether <s>Tathāgatas</s> do not arise, this nature of <s>dharmas</s> (phenomena) simply stands — one <s>dharma</s> is for the maintenance of beings, namely the four kinds of nutriment; two <s>dharmas</s> protect the world, namely moral shame and dread of blame,' and so forth. And also: 'There is coming from the other world to this world, and going from this world to the other world.' Thus <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>, characterized by cessation and so forth, has been taught by the <s>Bhagavān</s> — how then does it not cease? Since in this way arising and so forth are observed in <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>, therefore this <s>Madhyamaka</s> treatise was composed by the <s>Ācārya</s> for the purpose of showing the distinction between <s>sūtras</s> of provisional meaning (<s>neyārtha</s>) and definitive meaning (<s>nītārtha</s>). Therein, those arising and other [characteristics] that have been stated of <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> are not stated with reference to the intrinsic nature (<s>svabhāva</s>) that is the domain of one free from the darkness of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) and free from defilements; rather, they are stated with reference to the domain of knowledge that belongs to minds and eyes afflicted by the darkness of <s>avidyā</s>.

body.text: tattvadarśanāpekṣayā tūktaṃ bhagavatā- etaddhi bhikṣavaḥ paramaṃ satyaṃ yaduta amoṣadharma nirvāṇam, sarvasaṃskārāśca mṛṣā moṣadharmāṇaḥ iti | tathā- nāstyatra tathatā vā avitathatā vā | moṣadharmaka mapyetat, pralopadharmakamapyetat, mṛṣāpyetat, māyeyaṃ bālalāpinī iti | tathā-
body.translated_text: With reference to the vision of reality, however, the <s>Bhagavān</s> has stated: 'This indeed, monks, is the supreme truth, namely, <s>nirvāṇa</s>, which is of the nature of non-deception. All <s>saṃskāras</s> (formations) are false and of deceptive nature.' And also: 'There is no <s>tathatā</s> (suchness) or <s>avitathatā</s> (non-suchness) here. This too is of deceptive nature, of destructible nature, false — this <s>māyā</s> (illusion) is the prattle of fools.' And also —

children.translated_text: Form is like a mass of foam; feeling is like a bubble;
perception resembles a mirage; formations are like a plantain tree;
and consciousness is like an illusion — so declared the Kinsman of the Sun. //
A monk who thus examines <s>dharmas</s>, vigorous in his effort,

children.text: divā vā yadi vā rātrau saṃprajānan pratismṛtaḥ |
children.translated_text: whether by day or by night, clearly comprehending and mindful,
should penetrate the peaceful state — the quiescence of formations, the auspicious. //

body.text: nirātmakatvācca dharmāṇāmityādi ||
body.translated_text: And because <s>dharmas</s> are devoid of self (<s>nirātmaka</s>), and so forth.

body.text: yasyaivaṃ deśanābhiprāyānabhijñatayā saṃdehaḥ syāt- kā hyatra deśanā tattvārthā, kā nu khalu ābhiprāyikīti, yaścāpi mandabuddhitayā neyārthāṃ deśanāṃ nītārthāmavagacchati, tayorubhayorapi vineyajanayoḥ ācāryo yuktyāgamābhyāṃ saṃśayamithyājñānāpākaraṇārthaṃ śāstramidamārabdhavān ||
body.translated_text: For one who, through not understanding the intent of such teaching, has doubt — 'Which teaching here conveys the ultimate meaning, and which is intentional?' — and also for one who, through dull intelligence, understands a teaching of provisional meaning as one of definitive meaning — for both these types of persons to be trained, the <s>Ācārya</s> undertook this treatise in order to remove doubt and wrong understanding through reasoning (<s>yukti</s>) and scripture (<s>āgama</s>).

body.text: tatra 'na svataḥ'; ityādinā yuktirupavarṇitā ||
body.translated_text: Therein, by 'not from itself' and so forth, reasoning has been set forth.

children.translated_text: 'That is false, of deceptive nature' — so the <s>Bhagavān</s> declared.

children.text: sarve ca moṣadharmāṇaḥ saṃskārāstena te mṛṣā ||
children.translated_text: 'And all <s>saṃskāras</s> are of deceptive nature; therefore they are false.' //
'The prior limit is not known' — so spoke the Great Sage.
'<s>Saṃsāra</s> is without beginning or end; there is neither a first nor a last.' //
And in the <s>Kātyāyanāvavāda</s>, both 'it exists' and 'it does not exist'
were rejected by the <s>Bhagavān</s>, who discerns being and non-being. //

body.text: ityādinā āgamo varṇitaḥ ||
body.translated_text: By such [verses], scripture (<s>āgama</s>) has been set forth.

body.text: uktaṃ ca āryākṣayamatisūtre-
body.translated_text: And it is said in the noble <s>Akṣayamatisūtra</s>:

body.text: katame sūtrāntā neyārthāḥ katame nītārthāḥ? ye sūtrāntā mārgavatārāya nirdiṣṭāḥ, ima ucyanteḥ neyārthāḥ | ye sūtrāntāḥ phalāvatārāya nirdiṣṭāḥ, ima ucyante neyārthāḥ | yāvad ye sūtrāntāḥ śūnyatānimittāpraṇihitānabhisaṃskārājātānutpādābhāvanirātmaniḥ sattvanirjīvaniḥ pudgalāsvāmikavimokṣamukhā nirdiṣṭāḥ ta ucyante nītārthāḥ | iyamucyate bhadanta śāradvatīputra nītārthasūtrāntapratiśaraṇatā, na neyārthasūtrāntapratiśaraṇatā iti ||
body.translated_text: 'Which <s>sūtras</s> are of provisional meaning and which are of definitive meaning? Those <s>sūtras</s> taught for the purpose of entering the path — these are called of provisional meaning.
