body.text: yāvanmāreṇa pāpīyasā udake 'ntardhāpite athāsyaitadabhūt- yannvahamātmanaḥ kāyaṃ viddhā ime pṛthivīpradeśaṃ rudhireṇa siñceyam | tatkasya hetoḥ? ayaṃ pṛthivīpradeśa uddhatarajaskaḥ, mā rajodhāturito dharmodgatasya bodhisattvasya mahāsattvasya śarīre nipatet | kimahamātmabhāvena kariṣyāmi avaśyaṃ bhedanadharmiṇā? varaṃ khalu punarmama evaṃrūpayā kriyayā ātmabhāvasya vināśaḥ kṛto bhavet, na tvevaṃ niḥsāmarthyakriyayā | bahūni ca mama ātmabhāvasahasrāṇi kāmahetoḥ kāmanidānaṃ bhinnāni punaḥ punaḥ saṃsāre saṃsarataḥ, na punarevaṃbhūteṣu sthāneṣu ..... | atha khalu sadāprarudito bodhisattvo mahāsattvaḥ tīkṣṇaṃ śastraṃ gṛhītvā samantādātmānaṃ viddhā samantatastaṃ pṛthivīpradeśaṃ svakena rudhireṇāsiñcadityādi ||
body.translated_text: When water had been made to disappear by the evil <s>Māra</s>, then this thought occurred to him: 'Let me pierce my own body and sprinkle this region of earth with blood. For what reason? This region of earth is dusty; let not the dust-particles fall upon the body of the <s>Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata</s>. What shall I do with this body that is certainly subject to destruction? Better indeed that the destruction of my body be accomplished through such an action than through an action of powerlessness. And many thousands of my bodies have been destroyed again and again while wandering in <s>saṃsāra</s>, on account of sensual desire, for the sake of sensual desire — but never in such circumstances...' Then the <s>Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita</s>, having taken a sharp weapon, pierced himself all around and sprinkled that region of earth all around with his own blood — and so forth.

body.text: atha khalu sadāprarudito bodhisattvo mahāsattvaḥ sahadarśanādeva dharmodgatasya bodhisattvasya mahāsattvasya evaṃrūpaṃ sukhaṃ pratyalabhata- tadyathāpi nāma prathamadhyānasamāpannasya bhikṣorekāgramanasikārasya bhikṣoḥ | tatreyaṃ dharmodgatasya bodhisattvasya mahāsattvasya prajñāpāramitādeśanā yaduta sarvadharmasamatayā prajñāpāramitāsamatā, sarvadharmaviviktatayā prajñāpāramitāviviktatā, sarvadharmācalatayā prajñāpāramitācalatā, sarvadharmāmananatayā prajñāpāramitāmananatā, sarvadharmāstambhitatayā prajñāpāramitāstambhitatā, sarvadharmaikarasatayā prajñāpāramitaikarasatā, sarvadharmāparyantatayā prajñāpāramitāparyantatā, sarvadharmānutpādatayā prajñāpāramitānutpādatā, sarvadharmānirodhatayā prajñāpāramitānirodhatā, gaganāparyantatayā prajñāpāramitāparyantatā, yāvat sarvadharmāsaṃbhedanatayā prajñāpāramitāsaṃbhedanatā, sarvadharmānupalabdhitayā prajñāpāramitānupalabdhitā, sarvadharmābhibhāvanāsamatayā prajñāpāramitābhibhāvanāsamatā, sarvadharmaniśceṣṭatayā prajñāpāramitāniśceṣṭatā, sarvadharmācintyatayā prajñāpāramitācintyatā veditavyeti ||
body.translated_text: Then the <s>Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita</s>, at the very moment of seeing the <s>Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata</s>, experienced such happiness as a monk who has attained the first <s>dhyāna</s>, a monk of one-pointed attention. And therein, this was the teaching of the <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s> by the <s>Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata</s>: namely, through the equality of all <s>dharmas</s>, the equality of <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>; through the seclusion of all <s>dharmas</s>, the seclusion of <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>; through the immovability of all <s>dharmas</s>, the immovability of <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>; through the non-deliberation of all <s>dharmas</s>, the non-deliberation of <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>; through the non-fixity of all <s>dharmas</s>, the non-fixity of <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>; through the single-taste of all <s>dharmas</s>, the single-taste of <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>; through the boundlessness of all <s>dharmas</s>, the boundlessness of <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>; through the non-arising of all <s>dharmas</s>, the non-arising of <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>; through the non-cessation of all <s>dharmas</s>, the non-cessation of <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>; through the boundlessness of space, the boundlessness of <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>; up to: through the non-breaking of all <s>dharmas</s>, the non-breaking of <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>; through the non-apprehensibility of all <s>dharmas</s>, the non-apprehensibility of <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>; through the equality of the non-manifestation of all <s>dharmas</s>, the equality of the non-manifestation of <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>; through the inactivity of all <s>dharmas</s>, the inactivity of <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>; through the inconceivability of all <s>dharmas</s>, the inconceivability of <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s> — thus it should be known.

body.text: ityācāryacandrakīrtipādoparacitāyāṃ prasannapadāyāṃ madhyamakavṛttau ātmaparīkṣā nāma aṣṭādaśamaṃ prakaraṇam ||
body.translated_text: Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, 'Examination of the Self' (<s>Ātmaparīkṣā</s>), in the <s>Prasannapadā</s>, the <s>Madhyamaka</s> commentary composed by the venerable <s>Ācārya Candrakīrti</s>. //

body.text:
19
kālaparīkṣā ekonaviṃśatitamaṃ prakaraṇam |
body.translated_text:
19
'Examination of Time' (<s>Kālaparīkṣā</s>), the nineteenth chapter.

body.text: atrāha- vidyata eva bhāvānāṃ svabhāvaḥ, kālatrayavijñaptihetutvāt | iha atītānāgatapratyutpannāsrayaḥ kālā bhagavatā upadiṣṭāḥ | te ca bhāvāśrayāḥ | yasmādutpanno niruddho hi bhāvasvabhāvaḥ atīta iti vyapadiśyate, utpanno 'niruddho hi vartamānaḥ, alabdhātmabhāvo 'nāgata iti | evaṃ bhāvasvabhāvanibandhanāsrayaḥ kālā upadiṣṭāḥ | te ca santi | tasmāt tannibandhano 'pi bhāvasvabhāvo 'stīti | ucyate | syāt kālatrayaprajñaptiheturbhāvasvabhāvaḥ, yadi kālatrayameva bhavadabhimataṃ bhavet | na tvasti | yathā ca nāsti, tathā pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: Here the opponent says: The inherent nature of entities does indeed exist, because of the fact that the triad of times serves as the ground of designation. Here, the times based on past, future, and present have been taught by the <s>Bhagavān</s>. And these are based on entities. Since the inherent nature of an entity that has arisen and has ceased is designated as 'past,' that which has arisen and has not ceased is 'present,' and that which has not yet attained existence is 'future' — thus the times are taught as having the inherent nature of entities as their basis. And they exist. Therefore the inherent nature of entities, which is their basis, also exists. [Reply:] The inherent nature of entities would be the ground for the designation of the three times, if and only if the triad of times as you intend it were to exist. But it does not. And to demonstrate how it does not exist, [the <s>Ācārya</s>] says:

children.translated_text: If the present and the future depend on the past,
then the present and the future will exist in the past time. // 1 //

body.text: iha tāvat yadi vartamānānāgatau syātām, tāvapekṣya atītaṃ kālaṃ bhavetām, anapekṣya vā? tatra yadi atītamapekṣya sidhyete, tathā niyatamatīte kāle bhaviṣyataḥ | yasmāt, yasya hi yatra asattvam, tat tena nāpekṣyate| tadyathā vandhyā srī svatanayena, gaganamālatīlatā svakusumena, sikatā svatailena | avidyamānamapyandhakāraṃ pradīpena, pradīpo 'pi andhakāreṇa pratidvandvitvena apekṣyate iti cet, naitadevam | asyāpi sādhyasamatvāt | tadatra yadi atīte kāle vartamānānāgatau kālau iṣyete, apekṣāsiddhayarthamevaṃ sati atīte kāle vidyamānatvāt atītakālātmavat tayorapyatītatvaṃ syāt | tataśca atīto 'pi na syāt | yasmāt vartamānāvasthātikrānto hi atītaḥ asaṃprāptaḥ anāgata iti syāt | yadā tu vartamānānāgatayorasaṃbhava eva, tadā kutaḥ kasyacidatītatvaṃ syāt? ityataḥ atīto 'pi na syāt || 1 ||
body.translated_text: Here, first: if the present and the future were to exist, would they exist in dependence on the past time, or independently? In the first case, if they are established in dependence on the past, then they will necessarily exist in the past time. Because that which does not exist somewhere is not dependent on that — just as a barren woman [is not dependent on] her own son, [the] sky on a jasmine vine's own blossom, or sand on its own oil. [Objection:] Even though non-existent, darkness is dependent on a lamp, and a lamp too on darkness, through opposition. [Reply:] This is not so, since this too is equally unproven. Therefore here, if the present and future times are accepted [as existing] in the past time, then since they exist in the past time, they too would be of the nature of the past, just like the past time [itself]. And then the past too would not exist. For the 'past' is that which has transcended the present state; the 'future' would be that which has not yet arrived. But when the present and future are impossible [in the past], then how could anything be past? Therefore the past too would not exist. // 1 //

body.text: atha yathoktadoṣaparijihīrṣayā-
body.translated_text: Now, wishing to avoid the stated fault —

children.translated_text: If, on the other hand, the present and the future do not exist therein,
then how could the present and the future be dependent on that [past]? // 2 //

body.text: tatra atīte kāle yadi vartamānānāgatau kālau na staḥ iti parikalpyate, evamapi tatra avidyamānatvāt gaganendīvaravannāstyapekṣā || 2 ||
body.translated_text: If it is conceived that the present and future times do not exist in the past time, then even so, since they do not exist therein, there is no dependence — like a blue lotus in the sky. // 2 //

body.text: athāpi syāt- kālavādināṃ vidyate eva kālaḥ, tatra kimapekṣayā prayojanamiti? ucyate | evamapi-
body.translated_text: Moreover, one might say: for proponents of time, time does indeed exist — what need is there for dependence? [Reply:] Even so —

children.translated_text: Without dependence, the establishment of those two
apart from the past does not exist; therefore the present and the future, and hence time, does not exist. // 3 //

body.text: pratyutpannānāgatayorasattvam, atītānapekṣatvāt, kharaviṣāṇavat | yataścaivam pratyutpanno 'nāgataśca tasmātkālo na vidyate iti vijñeyam || 3 ||
body.translated_text: The non-existence of the present and the future [follows] from their not depending on the past — like a hare's horn. And since this is so, 'therefore the present and future, and hence time, does not exist' — this should be understood. // 3 //

body.text: yadā caivam atītamapekṣya vā anapekṣya vā pratyutpannānāgatayornāsti siddhiḥ, evaṃ pratyutpannāpekṣayā vā anapekṣayā vā atītānāgatayoḥ anāgatāpekṣayā vā anapekṣayā vā pratyutpannātītayoḥ asiddhau iṣyamāṇāyāṃ tenaiva pratyutpannāgatayoḥ atītāpekṣayā vā anapekṣayā asiddhikrameṇa dūṣaṇasāmyamatidiśannāha-
body.translated_text: And since in this way, whether in dependence on or independently of the past, the establishment of the present and future is not possible — in the same way, whether in dependence on or independently of the present, the establishment of the past and future [is not possible]; and whether in dependence on or independently of the future, the establishment of the present and past [is not possible]. Extending by the very same method of refutation used for the present and future in dependence on or independently of the past, to the remaining two [permutations], [the <s>Ācārya</s>] says:

children.translated_text: By this very [method], the remaining two [pairs] in their respective permutations,
and [the concepts of] upper, lower, and middle, unity, and so forth, should be discerned. // 4 //

body.text: kathaṃ kṛtvā?
body.translated_text: How so?

children.translated_text: If the past and the future depend on the present,
then the past time and the future will exist in the present.
If the past time and the future do not exist therein,
then how could the past time and the future be dependent on that [present]?

children.text: anapekṣya punaḥ siddhirna jātaṃ vidyate tayoḥ |
children.translated_text: Without dependence, the establishment of those two apart from the present does not exist;
therefore the past and the future — time does not exist. //

body.text: eṣa tāvadekaḥ kālaparivartaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the first permutation of time.

children.translated_text: If the past and the present depend on the unborn [i.e. the future],
then the past and the present will exist in the time of the unborn [future].
If the past and the present do not exist therein,
then how could the past and the present be dependent on that [future]?
Without dependence, the establishment of those two apart from the unborn [future] does not exist;
therefore the past and the present — time does not exist. //

body.text: eṣa dvitīyaḥ kālaparivarta iti vyākhyānakārikā iti | evaṃdvau kālaparivartau boddhavyau ||
body.translated_text: This is the second chapter on time — thus the explanatory verses. In this way, two chapters on time should be understood.

body.text: yataśca evaṃ vicāraṇe kālatrayaṃ nāsti, tasmāt kālo na vidyate, kālābhāvācca bhāvasadbhāvo 'pi nāsti iti siddham ||
body.translated_text: And since, upon such investigation, the three times do not exist, therefore time does not exist. And from the non-existence of time, the existence of entities too does not hold — this is established.

body.text:
yathā caitatkālatrayaṃ vicāritam, evam
uttamādhamamadhyādīnekatvādīṃśca lakṣayet |
body.translated_text:
And just as these three times have been investigated, even so —
'One should examine the superior, inferior, and middling, and so forth, as well as unity and so forth.' /

body.text: uttamādhamamadhyamān iti ādiśabdena kuśalākuśalāvyākṛtāni, utpādasthitibhaṅgāḥ, pūrvāntāparāntamadhyāntāḥ, kāmarūpārūpyadhātavaḥ, śaikṣāśaikṣanaivaśaikṣanaivāśaikṣādayo yāvantaḥ padārthāḥ tripadārthasaṃbandhavyavasthitāḥ, te sarve gṛhyante | ekatvādīṃśca ityanena ādiśabdena dvitvabahutvayo grahaṇāt te eva uttamādayaḥ ekatvādayaśca kālatrayavyākhyānena vyākhyātā veditavyāḥ || 4 ||
body.translated_text: 'Superior, inferior, and middling' — by the word 'and so forth,' the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; arising, duration, and destruction; the past limit, future limit, and middle limit; the desire-realm, form-realm, and formless-realm; the learner, the one beyond learning, the neither-learner-nor-beyond-learning, and the not-neither-learner-nor-beyond-learning — all these entities that are established through the relationship of three categories are included. And by 'unity and so forth,' since duality and multiplicity are included through the word 'and so forth,' these very [categories] — superior and so forth, as well as unity and so forth — should be understood as explained by the explanation of the three times. // 4 //

body.text: atrāha- vidyata eva kālaḥ parimāṇavattvāt | iha yannāsti, na tasya parimāṇavattvaṃ vidyate tadyathā kharaviṣāṇasya | asti ca kālasya parimāṇavattvaṃ kṣaṇalavamuhūrtadivasarātryahorātrapakṣamāsasaṃvatsarādibhedena | tasmāt, parimāṇavattvād vidyata eva kālaḥ iti | ucyate | yadi kālo nāma kaścit syāt, syāttasya parimāṇavattvam | na tvasti | yasmāt-
body.translated_text: Here one objects: time does indeed exist, because of having measurability. Here, what does not exist does not have measurability — just as a hare's horn. But time does have measurability, through the divisions of moment, unit-of-time, hour, day, night, day-and-night, fortnight, month, year, and so forth. Therefore, because of having measurability, time does indeed exist. It is replied: if there were something called time, it would have measurability. But there is not. Because —

children.text: nāsthito gṛhyate kālaḥ sthitaḥ kālo na vidyate |
children.translated_text: Time that is non-abiding is not apprehended; abiding time is not found. /
And how could time that is unapprehended be designated? // 5 //

body.text: iha yadi kālo nāma kaścidavasthitaḥ kṣaṇādivyatiriktaḥ syāt, sa kṣaṇādibhiḥ parimāṇavattvād gṛhyeta | na tu avasthitaḥ kūṭasthaḥ kaścit kālo nāma asti, yaḥ kṣaṇādibhirgṛhyeta | tadevaṃ nāsthito gṛhyate kālaḥ, asthitatvānna gṛhyate ityarthaḥ ||
body.translated_text: Here, if there were some time that existed as abiding, separate from moments and so forth, it would be apprehended through the measurability of moments and so forth. But there is no abiding, immutable thing called time that would be apprehended through moments and so forth. Thus, 'non-abiding time is not apprehended' — the meaning is: because of non-abidingness, it is not apprehended.

body.text: athāpi syāt- nitya eva avasthitasvabhāvaḥ kālo nāma asti, kṣaṇādibhirabhivyajyate | tathāhi-
body.translated_text: Now one might say: there is indeed a thing called time, having an abiding nature, which is eternal, and is manifested by moments and so forth. For thus —

body.text:
kālaḥ pacati bhūtāni kālaḥ saṃharate prajāḥ |
kālaḥ supteṣu jāgarti kālo hi duratikramaḥ || iti |
body.translated_text:
'Time ripens beings; time gathers creatures together; /
time is awake when [beings] are asleep; for time is indeed difficult to overcome.' //

body.text: yaścaivaṃlakṣaṇaḥ so 'vasthitasvabhāvo 'stīti | ucyate | evamapi sthitaḥ kālo na vidyate yaḥ kṣaṇādibhirabhivyajyamāno gṛhyeta | kasmāt punaḥ sthitaḥ kālo nāstīti cet, kṣaṇādivyatirekeṇāgṛhyamāṇatvāt ||
body.translated_text: — and one of such characteristics has an abiding nature, [one might say]. It is replied: even so, abiding time is not found that would be apprehended as being manifested by moments and so forth. Why is abiding time non-existent? Because it is not apprehended apart from moments and so forth.

body.text: api ca | ayaṃ kālaḥ saṃskṛtasvabhāvaḥ san astīti, asaṃskṛtasvabhāvo vā? ubhayaṃ ca saṃskṛtaparīkṣāyāṃ pratiṣiddham-
body.translated_text: Moreover, does this time exist as having a conditioned nature, or an unconditioned nature? Both have been negated in the Examination of the Conditioned —

children.translated_text: 'When arising, duration, and destruction are not established, the conditioned does not exist. /
And when the conditioned is not established, how will the unconditioned be established?' //

body.text: ityanena | tadevaṃ nāsti vyavasthitaḥ kālaḥ, yo gṛhyeta | yaśca idānīṃ kālo na gṛhyate asthitatvādavidyamānasvarūpatvāt, so 'gṛhyamāṇaḥ san kathaṃ kṣaṇādibhiḥ prajñapayituṃ bhāvataḥ pāryata ityāha- agṛhītaśca kālaḥ prajñapyate kathamiti | tasmānnāstyeva kālaḥ || 5 ||
body.translated_text: — by this. Thus, there is no established time that would be apprehended. And the time that is now not apprehended — because of non-abidingness, because of the non-existence of its own form — how can it, being unapprehended, be designated by moments and so forth as actually existing? He says: 'And how could time that is unapprehended be designated?' Therefore, time simply does not exist. // 5 //

body.text: atrāha- satyaṃ nāsti nityaḥ kālo nāma kaścid rūpādivyatiriktaḥ svabhāvasiddhaḥ, kiṃ tarhi rūpādīneva sa saṃskārānupādāya prajñaptaḥ kālaḥ kṣaṇādivācyo bhavati, tasmādadoṣa iti | ucyate | evamapi-
body.translated_text: Here one objects: it is true that there is no eternal thing called time, established by its own nature and separate from form and so forth. Rather, it is designated as time, expressible by moment and so forth, in dependence on just those <s>saṃskāras</s> (formations) such as form and so forth. Therefore there is no fault. It is replied: even so —

body.text: bhāvaṃ pratītya kālaścetkālo bhāvādṛte kutaḥ |
body.translated_text: If time exists in dependence on an entity, then whence is time apart from an entity? /

body.text: yadyevaṃ bhāvaṃ pratītya kālo bhavatīti bhavatā vyavasthāpyate, yadā khalu bhāvo nāsti, tadā niyataṃ taddhetuko 'pi kālo nāstīti pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: If time is thus established by you as existing in dependence on an entity, then when indeed the entity does not exist, time too, which is caused by it, certainly does not exist — demonstrating this, he says —

body.text: na ca kaścana bhāvo 'sti
body.translated_text: And no entity whatsoever exists. /

body.text: iti pūrvaṃ vistareṇa pratipāditatvādvakṣyamāṇapratiṣedhācca | yadā caivaṃ na kaścidbhāvo 'sti bhāvataḥ, tadā-
body.translated_text: — because this has been previously demonstrated at length, and because of the negation that will be stated. And when thus no entity whatsoever exists in reality, then —

body.text: kutaḥ kālo bhaviṣyati || 6 ||
body.translated_text: Whence will time come to be? // 6 //

body.text: kālābhāvācca na santi kṣaṇalavamuhūrtādayaḥ kālabhedāḥ tatpariṇāmabhūtāḥ, ityataḥ kutaḥ pariṇāmavattvena kālasiddhirbhaviṣyati? tasmānnāstyeva bhāvānāṃ svabhāvaḥ iti || uktaṃ hi bhagavatā āryahastikakṣyasūtre-
body.translated_text: And from the non-existence of time, the temporal divisions of moment, unit-of-time, hour, and so forth, which are transformations of it, do not exist. Hence, whence will the establishment of time through having transformations come to be? Therefore, the intrinsic nature of entities simply does not exist. For the <s>Bhagavān</s> has said in the Noble <s>Hastikakṣyasūtra</s> —

body.text:
yadi koci dharmāṇa bhavetsvabhāvaḥ tatraiva gaccheya jinaḥ saśrāvako |
kūṭasthadharmāṇa siyā na nirvṛtī na niṣprapañco bhavi jātu paṇḍitaḥ || iti |
body.translated_text:
'If <s>dharmas</s> had any intrinsic nature, the <s>Jina</s> together with his <s>Śrāvakas</s> would go there. /
For <s>dharmas</s> that are immutable, there would be no <s>nirvāṇa</s>, nor would a wise one ever be free from conceptual proliferation.' //

body.text: tathā-
body.translated_text: Likewise —

body.text:
buddhasahasraśatā ya atītā dharmasahasraśatāni bhaṇitvā |
naiva ca dharma na cākṣara kṣīṇā nāsti samudbhavu tena akṣīṇā || iti |
body.translated_text:
'The hundreds of thousands of <s>Buddhas</s> who have passed, having spoken hundreds of thousands of <s>dharmas</s> — /
neither <s>dharma</s> nor syllable has been exhausted, nor is there arising; therefore they are unexhausted.' //

body.text: tathā-
body.translated_text: Likewise —

children.text: utpādakāle hi tathāgatasya maitreyanāmā tviha yo bhaviṣyati |
children.translated_text: 'At the time of the arising of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the one named <s>Maitreya</s> who will be here — /

children.text: bhaviṣyatīyaṃ kanakāvṛtā mahī tasyā idānīṃ kuta āgamo 'sau ||
children.translated_text: this earth will be covered with gold; whence, then, is its coming now?' //

body.text: ullāpanāḥ kāmaguṇā hi pañca vibhrāmaṇā mohana moṣadharmiṇaḥ |
body.translated_text: 'The five qualities of sense-desire are indeed enticements, beguiling, deluding, and of the nature of robbery. /

body.text: madhyāhnakāle hi yathaiva grīṣme jalaṃ marīcyāṃ hi tathaiva kāmāḥ ||
body.translated_text: Just as water [appears] in a mirage at midday in summer — even so are sense-desires.' //

body.text: ekena kalpena bhaveddhi loko ākāśabhūto gaganasvabhāvo |
body.translated_text: 'In one <s>kalpa</s> (aeon), the world would become space-like, having the nature of the sky. /

body.text: dāhaṃ vināśaṃ ca payānti bhe[bhī?]ravaḥ kuta āgamaḥ kutra gatiśca teṣām || iti ||
body.translated_text: The fearsome ones experience burning and destruction — whence is their coming, and where is their going?' //

body.text: tadyathā-
body.translated_text: It is thus —

body.text: pañcemāni bhikṣavaḥ saṃjñāmātraṃ pratijñāmātraṃ vyavahāramātraṃ saṃvṛtimātraṃ yaduta atīto 'dhvā anāgato 'dhvā ākāśaṃ nirvāṇaṃ pudgalaśceti ||
body.translated_text: 'These five, monks, are mere concepts, mere conventions, mere designations, mere conventions: namely, the past course, the future course, space, <s>nirvāṇa</s>, and the person (<s>pudgala</s>).'

body.text: || ityācāryacandrakīrtipādoparacitāyāṃ prasannapadāyāṃ madhyamakavṛttau kālaparīkṣā nāma ekonaviṃśaṃ prakaraṇam ||
body.translated_text: Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, 'The Examination of Time,' in the <s>Prasannapadā</s>, the <s>Madhyamaka</s> commentary composed by <s>Ācārya Candrakīrtipāda</s>.

body.text:
20
sāmagrīparīkṣā viṃśatitamaṃ prakaraṇam |
body.translated_text:
20
The Examination of the Assemblage (<s>Sāmagrīparīkṣā</s>), the Twentieth Chapter.

body.text: atrāha- vidyate kālaḥ, phalapravṛttau sahakārikāraṇabhāvāt | yo nāsti, nāsau sahakārikāraṇabhāvena pratipadyate, vandhyātanayavat | tasmādasti kālaḥ, sahakārikāraṇabhāvāt | iha bījāvanisalilajvalanapavanagaganābhidhānahetupratyayasāmagrīṃ pratītya ayamaṅkura upajāyamānaḥ satyāmapi bījādipratyayasāmagryām, ṛtuviśeṣāsaṃnidhānānnopajāyate | yathā ca bāhyeṣu, evamādhyātmikeṣvapi | yathoktaṃ bhagavatā-
body.translated_text: Here one objects: time does indeed exist, because of functioning as a cooperating cause for the production of the fruit. What does not exist does not function as a cooperating cause — like the son of a barren woman. Therefore time exists, because of functioning as a cooperating cause. Here, when this sprout arises in dependence on the assemblage of causes and conditions designated as seed, earth, water, fire, wind, and space — even when the assemblage of conditions such as seed and so forth exists, it does not arise due to the non-presence of a particular season. And just as with external [things], so too with internal ones. As the <s>Bhagavān</s> has said —

children.translated_text: 'Actions do not perish even in hundreds of <s>koṭis</s> (ten millions) of <s>kalpas</s> (aeons). /

children.text: sāmagrīṃ prāpya kālaṃ ca phalanti khalu dehinām || iti ||
children.translated_text: Having reached the assemblage and the [right] time, they certainly bear fruit for embodied beings.' //

body.text: yasmācca evamasti kālāpekṣā, tasmādastyasau kālo nāma, yaḥ aṅkurādipravṛttau sahakārikāraṇaṃ bhavatīti | ucyate | syāt sahakārikāraṇatā kālasya, yadi aṅkurādiphalasya pravṛttireva syāt | na tvasti | kathaṃ kṛtvā? iha bījādihetupratyayasāmagrīto 'ṅkurādiphalodaye parikalpyamāne vyavasthitasya vā phalasya sāmagryāṃ satyāṃtata utpādaḥ parikalpyeta avyavasthitasya vā? kiṃ cātaḥ? yadi tāvad vyavasthitasya parikalpyate, tanna yujyate iti pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: And since there is thus dependence on time, therefore there does exist that thing called time, which functions as a cooperating cause in the production of sprout and so forth. It is replied: time would have the status of a cooperating cause, if there were indeed production of the fruit — namely, the sprout and so forth. But there is not. How so? Here, when the arising of the fruit such as the sprout from the assemblage of causes and conditions such as the seed is conceived — is its arising from the assemblage conceived for a fruit that is [already] established, or for one that is not established? What of that? If first it is conceived for one [already] established — that is not tenable — demonstrating this, he says —

children.text: hetośca pratyayānāṃ ca sāmagryā jāyate yadi |
children.translated_text: If from the assemblage of cause and conditions, [the fruit] arises — /

children.text: phalamasti ca sāmagryāṃ sāmagryā jāyate katham || 1 ||
children.translated_text: and the fruit exists in the assemblage — how is it born from the assemblage? // 1 //

body.text: yadi hetupratyayasāmagryāṃ tvanmatena phalamasti, nanu evaṃ sati yasmāt sāmagryāmasti, kathaṃ tayā tajjanyate? na hi kuṇḍe dadhi vidyamānaṃ kuṇḍena janyate | api ca | yadvidyate tanniṣpannatvāt niṣpannapurovasthitaghaṭavat na punarjanmāpekṣate | abhivyaktiḥ sthaulyaṃ vā sūkṣmātmanā vidyamānasya kriyata iti cet, tasyāpi pakṣasya pūrvameva-
body.translated_text: If, in your view, the fruit exists in the assemblage of causes and conditions, then since it exists in the assemblage, how is it born by it? For curds that already exist in a pot are not produced by the pot. Moreover, what [already] exists does not require a further birth, because of being already produced — like a pot that is already produced and present before [one]. If it is said that manifestation or grossness is produced for what exists in a subtle form — to this position too, the reply has been stated previously —

body.text: āgacchatyanyato nāgnirindhane 'gnirna vidyate |
body.translated_text: 'Fire does not come from elsewhere; fire is not found in fuel' — /

body.text: ityatroktamuttaram || 1 ||
body.translated_text: — at that point. // 1 //

body.text: atha nāstyeva sāmagryāṃ phalamiti parikalpyate, etadapi nopapadyate iti pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: Now, if it is conceived that the fruit simply does not exist in the assemblage — this too is not tenable — demonstrating this, he says —

children.text: hetośca pratyayānāṃ ca sāmagryā jāyate yadi |
children.translated_text: If from the assemblage of cause and conditions, [the fruit] arises — /

children.text: phalaṃ nāsti ca sāmagryāṃ sāmagryā jāyate katham || 2 ||
children.translated_text: and the fruit does not exist in the assemblage — how is it born from the assemblage? // 2 //

body.text: yadi hetośca pratyayānāṃ ca sāmagryāṃ nāsti tatphalam, kathaṃ tarhi hetupratyayasāmagryā phalaṃ janyate? tatra avidyamānatvāt sikatābhiriva tailam | ata eva asaṃbhāvayannāha-
body.translated_text: If the fruit does not exist in the assemblage of causes and conditions, then how does the assemblage of causes and conditions produce the fruit? Because of its non-existence there — like oil from sand. For this very reason, expressing incredulity, he says —

body.text: phalaṃ nāsti ca sāmagryāṃ sāmagryā jāyate katham |
body.translated_text: 'The fruit does not exist in the assemblage — how is it born from the assemblage?' /

body.text: na tatphalaṃ sāmagrīto jāyate ityabhiprāyaḥ || 2 ||
body.translated_text: The intended meaning is: that fruit is not born from the assemblage. // 2 //

body.text: kiṃ cānyat-
body.translated_text: And what else —

children.translated_text: If from the assemblage of causes and conditions, the fruit exists — /

children.text: gṛhyeta nanu sāmagryāṃ sāmagryāṃ ca na gṛhyate || 3 ||
children.translated_text: surely it should be apprehended in the assemblage; but it is not apprehended in the assemblage. // 3 //

body.text: yad yatra asti, tat tatra gṛhyate, tadyathā kuṇḍe dadhi | yacca yatra nāsti na tattatra gṛhyate tadyathā sikatāsu tailam, maṇḍūkajaṭāyāṃ śiromaṇiḥ ||
body.translated_text: What exists somewhere is apprehended there — for example, curds in a pot. And what does not exist somewhere is not apprehended there — for example, oil in sand, a crest-jewel on a frog's head-hair.

body.text: atha syāt- vidyamānā api padārthāḥ atisaukṣmyāt, atisaṃnikarṣāt, ativiprakarṣāt, indriyopaghātāt, mūrtivaddravyavyavadhānāt, mūrtyantardhānāt, manonavasthānāt, paramāṇuvat akṣasthāñjanaśalākāvat ādityagativat taimirikaikaikakeśavat andhabadhirādirūpaśabdādivat kuḍayādivyavahitaghaṭādivat siddhadevapiśācādiśarīravat viṣayāntaravyāpṛtasya viṣayāntaravanna gṛhyate iti cet, kiṃ khalu eṣāmagṛhyamāṇānāmastitve liṅgam, yena eṣāmastitve sati anupalabdhiriti syāt? anumānopamānāgamairgrahaṇādeṣāmastitvamiti cet, na tarhi teṣāmanupalabdhiriti vaktavyam, anumānādibhirupalabhyamānatvāt | yad rūpīndriyagrāhyaṃ tad ebhiḥ kāraṇairvidyamānamapi sanna gṛhyate, iti cet, ucyate | kimasmābhirevamuktam- rūpīndriyairvidyamānaṃ sad gṛhyeteti? kiṃ tarhi sāmānyenaiva yad brūmaḥ- gṛhyeta nanu sāmagryāmiti ||
body.translated_text: Now one might say: even things that exist may not be apprehended because of excessive subtlety, excessive proximity, excessive distance, damage to the sense-faculties, obstruction by a material substance, concealment by another material body, inattention of the mind — like atoms, like a collyrium-stick in the eye, like the course of the sun, like individual hairs [seen by] one with eye-disease, like form and sound for the blind and deaf, like a pot obstructed by a wall, like the bodies of <s>siddhas</s> (perfected beings), gods, and <s>piśācas</s> (spirits), and like [not perceiving] one sense-object when one is engaged with another sense-object. [Reply:] What indeed is the evidence for the existence of these unapprehended things, such that their non-apprehension would be [compatible with] their existence? If it is said: their existence is [known] through apprehension by inference, analogy, and scripture — then one should not say that they are 'not apprehended,' since they are apprehended through inference and so forth. [If it is said:] that which is graspable by the material sense-faculties, though existing, is not grasped due to these [listed] causes — it is replied: have we indeed said that what exists should be grasped by the material sense-faculties? What, then, do we say simply in general? 'Surely it should be apprehended in the assemblage.'

body.text: athāpi manyase- yad yatra nāsti, na tat tasmādutpadyate sikatābhyastailavat | utpadyate ca sāmagrītaḥ phalam, tasmādanumānataḥ sāmagryāṃ phalasyāstitvamiti | ucyate | yad yatra asti, na tat tasmādutpadyate, tadyathā kuṇḍād dadhi iti | asmādapyanumānādastitvamasya ayuktamiti kṛtvā nāstyeva sāmagryāṃ phalamiti kiṃ na gṛhyate?
body.translated_text: Now, if you think: what does not exist somewhere does not arise from that — like oil from sand; and the fruit does arise from the assemblage; therefore, by inference, the fruit exists in the assemblage — it is replied: what exists somewhere does not arise from that — for example, curds from a pot. From this inference too, the existence of this [fruit in the assemblage] is not correct — therefore, knowing that 'the fruit simply does not exist in the assemblage,' why is this not accepted?

body.text: athāpi syāt- ubhyorapi pakṣayoranumānavirodhād yathā astitvaṃ na yuktam, evaṃ nāstitvamapīti | ucyate | na vayamasyāsattvaṃ pratipādayāmaḥ, kiṃ tarhi paraparikalpitaṃ sattvamasya nirākurmaḥ | evaṃ na vayamasya sattvaṃ pratipādayāmaḥ, kiṃ tarhi paraparikalpitamasattvamasya apākurmaḥ | antadvayaparihāreṇa madhyamāyāḥ pratipadaḥ pratipādayitumiṣṭatvāditi | uktaṃ ca āryadevapādīye śatake-
body.translated_text: Now one might say: since there is a contradiction with inference in both positions, just as existence is not tenable, so too non-existence [is not tenable]. It is replied: we do not demonstrate the non-existence of this; rather, we refute the existence fabricated by the other party. Likewise, we do not demonstrate the existence of this; rather, we set aside the non-existence fabricated by the other party — because we wish to demonstrate the Middle Path by avoiding both extremes. And it has been said in the <s>Śataka</s> of the venerable <s>Āryadevapadā</s> —

body.text:
stambhādīnāmalaṃkāro gṛhasyārthe nirarthakaḥ |
satkāryameva yasyeṣṭaṃ yasyāsatkāryameva ca || iti |
body.translated_text:
'The ornament of pillars and the like is useless for the purpose of a house. /
[This applies to] one for whom the <s>satkāryavāda</s> (pre-existence of effect) alone is accepted, and one for whom the <s>asatkāryavāda</s> (non-pre-existence of effect) alone [is accepted].' //

body.text: tadevaṃ na sāmagrītaḥ phalamutpadyate vidyamānasya grahaṇaprasaṅgāt, iti vyavasthitam || 3 ||
body.translated_text: Thus, the fruit does not arise from the assemblage — because of the absurd consequence that what exists [therein] would be apprehended — this is established. // 3 //

body.text: atha manyase- nāstyeva sāmagryāṃ phalamiti, evamapi-
body.translated_text: Now, if you think that the fruit simply does not exist in the assemblage — even so —

children.text: hetośca pratyayānāṃ ca sāmagryāṃ nāsti cetphalam |
children.translated_text: If from the assemblage of causes and conditions, the fruit does not exist — /
causes and conditions would be the same as non-causes and non-conditions. // 4 //

body.text: yathā hi jvālāṅgārādiṣu aṅkuro nāstīti kṛtvā tasya te hetupratyayā na bhavanti, eva vivakṣitānāmapi bījādīnāṃ hetupratyayatā na syāt teṣu aṅkuro nāstīti kṛtvā | na ca ahetu pratyayebhyaḥ phalapravṛttiryukteti nāsti svabhāvataḥ phalapravṛttiḥ ||
body.translated_text: For just as flames, embers, and the like are not causes and conditions of a sprout because the sprout does not exist in them, even so, the intended seeds and the like too would not have the status of causes and conditions, because the sprout does not exist in them either. And since the production of a fruit from non-causes and non-conditions is not tenable, there is no production of fruit through <s>svabhāva</s> (inherent nature).

body.text: atrāha- naiva hi sāmagryāḥ phalotpādanasāmarthyamasti yataḥ iyaṃ cintā syāt- kiṃ sāmagryāṃ phalamasti utāho nāstīti | kiṃ tarhi hetoḥ phalotpādanasāmarthyam | sāmagrī tu hetoranugrahamātraṃ karoti | sa hetuḥ phalasyotpattyarthaṃ hetuṃ datvā nirudhyate, tena ca hetunā anugṛhyamāṇaṃ phalamutpadyate iti | ucyate | naiva hi ajātasya phalasya hetoranugrahaṇamasti | na cāpyajātasya bandhyātanayasyeva kenacitkiṃcinmātraṃ kartuṃ śakyamityayuktaiṣā kalpanā || 4 ||
body.translated_text: Here one objects: it is not the assemblage that has the capacity to produce the fruit, such that this question would arise — 'does the fruit exist in the assemblage or not?' Rather, the cause has the capacity to produce the fruit. The assemblage merely assists the cause. That cause, having given the causal factor for the sake of the fruit's production, ceases; and by that causal factor, the fruit, being assisted, arises. The reply is: there is certainly no assistance of the cause for a fruit that has not yet been born. And nothing whatsoever can be done for what has not been born, just as for a barren woman's son. Therefore this supposition is untenable. // 4 //

body.text: api ca-
body.translated_text: Moreover:

children.translated_text: If the cause ceases after having given the causal factor to the fruit, /
that which has been given and that which has ceased would be a twofold self of the cause. // 5 //

body.text: yadi hetuḥ phalasyotpattyarthaṃ hetukaṃ kāraṇaṃ datvā nirudhyata iti parikalpyate, evaṃ sati yaddattaṃ yanniruddhaṃ ca tadātmabhāvadvayaṃ hetoḥ syāt | na caitad yuktam, ardhaśāśvataprasaṅgāt nityānityayośca parasparaviruddhayorekatvābhāvāt || 5 ||
body.translated_text: If it is supposed that the cause ceases after having given the causal factor — the condition — for the sake of the fruit's production, then in that case, that which has been given and that which has ceased would be a twofold self-nature of the cause. But this is not tenable, because of the consequence of being half-eternal, and because there is no identity of the permanent and the impermanent, which are mutually contradictory. // 5 //

body.text: atha hetorātmabhāvadvayaprasaṅgaparihārārthaṃ sarvātmanā nirodha iṣyate phalasyotpattyarthaṃ kiṃcidapyadatvā, evamapi-
body.translated_text: Now, if, in order to avoid the consequence of a twofold self-nature of the cause, the cause is accepted as ceasing entirely without giving anything whatsoever for the sake of the fruit's production, even so:

children.translated_text: If the cause ceases without having given the causal factor to the fruit, /
the fruit, born when the cause has ceased, would be causeless. // 6 //

body.text: yadi phalasya kiṃcidapyadatvā sarvātmanā heturnirudhyate, nanu tasmin hetau niruddhe yatphalamutpadyate tat āhetukaṃ syāt | na ca āhetukamasti | ityayuktaiṣā kalpanā || 6 ||
body.translated_text: If the cause ceases entirely without giving anything whatsoever to the fruit, then surely that fruit which arises when the cause has ceased would be causeless. And nothing is causeless. Therefore this supposition is untenable. // 6 //

body.text: atrāha- yadi evaṃ phalasya hetorutpattau doṣaḥ, evaṃ sati sahotpannaiva sāmagrī phalasya janikā astu, tadyathā pradīpaprabhāyā iti | eṣāpi kalpanā nopapadyate iti pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: Here one objects: if there is a defect in the arising of the fruit from the cause in this way, then let the assemblage itself, co-arisen [with the fruit], be the producer of the fruit — just as with the light of a lamp. This supposition too is untenable — demonstrating this, he says:

children.translated_text: If the fruit were to appear simultaneously with the assemblage, /
it would follow that the producer and the produced are simultaneous. // 7 //

body.text: na caikakālayoḥ savyetaragoviṣāṇayorjanyajanakatvaṃ dṛṣṭam, vāmadakṣiṇakarayoścaraṇayorvā, ityayuktaiṣā kalpanā ityayuktametat || 7 ||
body.translated_text: And it is not observed that things existing at the same time — like the left and right horns of a cow, or the left and right hands or feet — have the relation of producer and produced. Therefore this supposition is untenable. // 7 //

body.text: atrāhureke- naiva hi abhūtvā bhāvānāmutpattiryuktā ākasmikatvaprasaṅgāt | tasmād hetupratyayasāmagrītaḥ pūrvameva tat phalamanāgatāvasthāyāṃ vyavasthitamanāgatātmanā | tasya hetupratyaya sāmagryā vartamānāvasthā janyate, dravyaṃ tu vyavasthitameveti | tān pratyucyate-
body.translated_text: Here some say: it is not tenable that entities arise having previously not existed, because of the consequence of arising accidentally. Therefore, that fruit, existing even prior to the assemblage of causes and conditions, is established in a future state with a future nature. Its present state is produced by the assemblage of causes and conditions, but the substance remains established as it is. To them it is replied:

children.translated_text: If the fruit existed even prior to the assemblage, /
the fruit, being independent of causes and conditions, would be causeless. // 8 //

body.text: yadi bhavatāmabhīpsitaṃ sāmagrītaḥ pūrvameva phalaṃ svarūpataḥ syāditi, tad hetupratyayanirapekṣaṃ syāt, tataśca āhetukaṃ syāt | na ca āhetukānāṃ padārthānāmastitvaṃ yuktam, kharaturagoragaviṣāṇādīnāmapyastitvaprasaṅgāt, pūrvasiddhasya ca punaḥ hetupratyayāpekṣayā niṣprayojanatvādityayuktametat || 8 ||
body.translated_text: If it is your desire that the fruit exists in its own form even prior to the assemblage, then it would be independent of causes and conditions, and therefore causeless. And the existence of causeless entities is not tenable, because donkey-horns and the like would also exist. And because what is already established has no purpose in depending again on causes and conditions — therefore this is untenable. // 8 //

body.text: anye punarvarṇayanti- hetureva phalaṃ janayati na sāmagrī | na ca uktadoṣaprasaṅgaḥ | yasmāt na hi anyohetuḥ anyat phalam | yataḥ, kiṃ hetuṃ datvā phalasya heturnirudhyate uta adatvaiveti vicāraḥ syāt | api tu hetureva niruddhaḥ phalātmanā vyavasthitaḥ iti | ucyate | evamapi-
body.translated_text: Others describe it thus: it is the cause itself that produces the fruit, not the assemblage. And the stated defects do not follow. Because the cause is not one thing and the fruit another. Hence the question — does the cause cease after giving something to the fruit, or without giving? — would not arise. Rather, the cause itself, having ceased, is established with the nature of the fruit. The reply is: even so —

children.text: niruddhe cetphalaṃ hetau hetoḥ saṃkramaṇaṃ bhavet |
children.translated_text: If the fruit [arises] when the cause has ceased, there would be a transference of the cause. /
And the consequence of the re-birth of a previously born cause would follow. // 9 //

body.text: yadi niruddhe hetau bhavanmatena phalamutpadyate, tacca phalaṃ hetvātmakameva bhavatīti parikalpyate, evaṃ sati hetoḥ saṃkramaṇaṃ bhavet, naṭasya veṣāntaraparityāgena veṣāntarasaṃcāravat hetoḥ saṃkramaṇa mātrameva syāt, na tu apūrvasya phalasyotpādaḥ | tataśca hetornityataiva syāt | na ca nityānāmastitvaṃ kvacidasti | yathoktaṃ śatake-
body.translated_text: If, according to your view, the fruit arises when the cause has ceased, and if that fruit is conceived as having the very nature of the cause, then in that case there would be a transference of the cause — just as an actor merely transitions from one costume to another without anything new being produced, so too there would be merely a transference of the cause, not the production of a new fruit. And therefore the cause would be permanent. But permanent things do not exist anywhere. As stated in the <s>Catuḥśataka</s>:

children.translated_text: 'Existence independent of conditions is never found, of anything, anywhere. /
Nothing anywhere is ever eternal.' //

body.text: kiṃ ca | etasyāṃ kalpanāyāṃ pūrvajātasya ca hetoḥ punarjanma prāpnoti | na ca jātasya punarapi [janma] yujyate niṣprayojanatvāt, anavasthāprasaṅgācca ||
body.translated_text: What is more, in this supposition, the consequence of the re-birth of a previously born cause would follow. And the re-birth of what has already been born is not tenable, because it is purposeless and because of the consequence of infinite regress.

body.text: atha manyase- yenātmanā vidyamāno na tenaivātmanā jāyate, yena cātmanā avidyamānaḥ tenaiva jāyata iti | etadapi na yuktam | aparityaktahetusvabhāvasya hetusvarūpasya phalamiti saṃjñāmātrabhedādavasthābhedācca dravyābhedasya sādhayitumaśakyatvāt | phalāvasthāyāṃ ca parityaktahetusvabhāvasya phalaśabdavācyatvād hetuḥ phalātmanā tiṣṭhatīti yatkiṃcidetat || 9 ||
body.translated_text: Now, one might think: it is not born with the very nature by which it existed [as cause]; rather, it is born with precisely the nature by which it did not exist [as cause]. This too is not correct — because, without having relinquished the <s>svabhāva</s> of the cause, the own-form of the cause cannot be demonstrated as different in substance merely through a difference in name or a difference in state by being called 'fruit.' And if, in the state of being a fruit, the <s>svabhāva</s> of the cause has been relinquished and it becomes expressible by the word 'fruit,' then the statement 'the cause persists with the nature of the fruit' is meaningless. // 9 //

body.text: kiṃ cānyat- yadi hetuḥ phalaṃ janayet, niruddho vā janayedaniruddho vā? phalamapi utpannaṃ vā janayedanutpannaṃ vā? ubhayathā ca nopapadyate iti pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: What is more: if the cause were to produce the fruit — would a ceased cause produce it, or an unceased one? And the fruit — would it produce an arisen one, or an unarisen one? In both cases it is untenable — demonstrating this, he says:

children.translated_text: How can a ceased, vanished cause produce a fruit that has [already] arisen? /
And how can a cause, even while persisting, produce [a fruit] when it is sustained by [an already existent] fruit? // 10 //

body.text: yadi tāvata niruddhaḥ astaṃgataḥ hetuḥ utpannaṃ sat vidyamānaṃ phalaṃ janayatīti parikalpyate, tannopapadyate | kasmāditi cet, kathaṃ niruddhaḥ asaṃvidyamānaḥ hetuḥ phalaṃ janayet? yadi janayati, vandhyāputro 'pi putraṃ janayiṣyati | phalaṃ ca sad vidyamānamapi janmanirapekṣamapi kathaṃ heturjanayi ṣyati? atha manyase- śaktyabhāvānniruddho na janayati, kiṃ tu tiṣṭhanneva hetuḥ phalaṃ janayiṣyatīti | ucyate |
body.translated_text: If it is supposed that a ceased, vanished cause produces an existent, present fruit, that is not tenable. Why? Because how can a ceased, non-existent cause produce a fruit? If it produces one, even a barren woman's son would produce a son. And the fruit, being existent and present, not needing birth — how can the cause produce it? Now, one might think: because of the absence of capacity, a ceased cause does not produce [a fruit

body.text: tiṣṭhannapi heturavikṛtarūpo vidyamānena phalena vṛtaḥ saṃbaddhaḥ kathaṃ janayet? iha hi-
body.translated_text: ; rather, the cause, while persisting, will produce the fruit. The reply is:] Even a persisting cause, being of unaltered form, sustained by — i.e., connected with — an existing fruit — how can it produce? For here:

body.text: kāraṇaṃ vikṛtiṃ gacchajjāyate 'nyasya kāraṇam |
body.translated_text: A cause produces another cause when it undergoes transformation. /

body.text: iti kāraṇābhāvaṃ pratipadyamānasya hetoravaśyaṃ vikāreṇa bhavitavyam | yastu na vikriyate, sa hetulakṣaṇayukta eva na bhavatīti | phalena ca saṃbaddhaḥ kathaṃ janayet? phalasya vidyamānatvāt || 10 ||
body.translated_text: A cause that is reaching its own non-existence must necessarily undergo transformation. But one that does not undergo transformation simply does not have the defining mark of being a cause. And how can it produce when it is connected with [an already existing] fruit — since the fruit is [already] existent? // 10 //

body.text: atha manyase- vidyamānasya phalasya punarjanayitumaśakyatvāt avṛta eva asaṃbaddha eva hetuḥ phalena phalaṃ janayiṣyatīti, etadapyayuktamityāha-
body.translated_text: Now, one might think: since an already existing fruit cannot be produced again, the cause, being uncovered by — i.e., unconnected with — a fruit, will produce the fruit. This too is untenable — hence he says:

body.text: athāvṛtaḥ phalenāsau katamajjanayetphalam |
body.translated_text: If [the cause] is uncovered by fruit, which fruit would it produce? /

body.text: yadi hetuḥ phalena asaṃbaddha eveṣyate, tadā katamadidānīṃ phalaṃ janayet? sarvameva vā phalaṃ janayedasaṃbaddhatvāt, na vā kiṃcijjanayedasaṃbaddhatvādevetyabhiprāyaḥ ||
body.translated_text: If the cause is accepted as simply unconnected with any fruit, then which fruit would it now produce? It would either produce every fruit whatsoever, because of being unconnected, or it would produce no fruit at all, because of being unconnected — this is the intended meaning.

body.text: kiṃ cānyat | yadi hetuḥ phalaṃ janayet, sa dṛṣṭvā phalaṃ janayedadṛṣṭvā vā? ubhayathā ca na yujyate ityāha-
body.translated_text: What is more: if the cause were to produce a fruit — would it produce it by seeing [it], or without seeing [it]? In both cases it is not tenable — hence he says:

body.text: na hyadṛṣṭvā vā dṛṣṭvā vā heturjanayate phalam || 11 ||
body.translated_text: For a cause produces a fruit neither without seeing nor by seeing. // 11 //

body.text: tatra yadi heturdṛṣṭvā janayatīti parikalpyate, tanna yujyate | yasmādvidyamānameva draṣṭuṃ pāryate nāvidyamānam | vidyamānaṃ cet, tanna janyate vidyamānatvāditi | evaṃ tāvad hetuḥ phalaṃ dṛṣṭvā na janayati, adṛṣṭvāpi na janayati, sarvasya phalasya hetorjanakatvaprasaṅgāt ||
body.translated_text: Therein, if it is supposed that the cause produces by seeing — that is not tenable. Because only what is existent can be seen, not what is non-existent. And if it is existent, it is not produced, because it [already] exists. Thus, a cause does not produce a fruit by seeing it. Nor does it produce without seeing, because of the consequence that the cause would produce every fruit.

body.text: atha kimidaṃ darśanaṃ kiṃ vā adarśanamiti? ucyate | prasiddhametalloke- upalabdhirdarśanamiti ||
body.translated_text: Now, what is this 'seeing,' and what is 'not seeing'? The reply is: this is well-established in the world — apprehension is seeing.

body.text: nanu etad bījādiṣu nirindriyeṣu na saṃbhavati | saṃbhavatu mā vā | nāsmākamayaṃ paryanuyogaḥ kiṃ tarhi tasyotpādavādinaḥ | tatra yaḥ utpādavādī brūyāt- dṛṣṭvā janayatīti, sa vaktavyaḥ- na dṛṣṭametalloke yadbījādikaṃ paśyatīti | tasmādayuktā eṣā kalpanā | atha adṛṣṭvā kalpayet, evamapi yatkiṃcidadṛṣṭaṃ saṃbhavati tatsarvamutpādayet, na cotpādayati, tasmāt na adṛṣṭvāpi janayati | aniṣṭāpattyā hi vayaṃ parakalpanāṃ vicārayāmaḥ saṃsārāṭavīkāntāragiridarīprapātaduḥkhamālāsamākulāmā tāmīva | buddhipūrvakartṛkaṃ ca puruṣādikāraṇino jagadabhyupagacchanto nirgranthāścaikendriyaṃ bījādikaṃ pratipannāḥ prasaṅgānna vyativartanta iti | tasmānnāsti doṣaḥ || 11 ||
body.translated_text: But surely this is not possible for seeds and the like, which are devoid of sense-faculties! Let it be possible or not — this objection does not apply to us, but rather to the proponent of production. Therein, if a proponent of production were to say 'it produces by seeing,' he must be told: it is not observed in the world that a seed and the like sees. Therefore this supposition is untenable. And if he supposes 'without seeing,' even so, whatever is not seen but nonetheless comes into being would produce everything — but it does not produce [everything]. Therefore it does not produce without seeing either. For we examine the other's supposition through the consequence of undesired results — like a mother in the jungle of <s>saṃsāra</s>, beset by a garland of sufferings from precipices in the mountain-caves. And those who accept an intelligent agent — such as <s>Puruṣa</s> (Person) and the like — as the cause of the world, and also the <s>Nirgranthas</s> who accept seeds and the like as having a single sense-faculty — they too do not escape from these consequences. Therefore there is no defect [in our position]. // 11 //

body.text: kiṃ cānyat- yadi yuṣmadabhimataṃ hetoḥ phalasya ca anyonyaḍhaukanalakṣaṇaṃ saṃgamanaṃ syāt, syāttadānīṃ tayorjanyajanakabhāvaḥ | yasmāt na hi parasparāsaṃgatayorālokāndhakārayoḥ saṃsāranirvāṇa yorjanyajanakabhāvo dṛṣṭa iti | ataḥ avaśyaṃ hetuphalabhāvayorjanyajanakabhāvamicchatā pareṇa saṃgatirabhyupeyā | sā ca kālatraye 'pi vicāryamāṇā na saṃbhavati | ato hetuḥ phalaṃ na janayati | yathā ca saṃgatirnāsti tathā pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: What is more: if there existed a meeting of cause and fruit of the kind you intend — characterized by the mutual approach of cause and fruit — then there would be the relation of producer and produced between them. For the relation of producer and produced is not observed between things that are mutually unmet, like light and darkness, like <s>saṃsāra</s> and <s>nirvāṇa</s>. Therefore, the opponent who wishes for the relation of producer and produced between cause and fruit must necessarily accept their meeting. But this meeting, when examined in the three times, is impossible. Therefore the cause does not produce the fruit. Demonstrating how there is no meeting, he says:

children.translated_text: There is never a meeting of a past fruit with a past cause, /
nor with an unborn [cause], nor with a born [cause]. // 12 //

body.text: atītasya tāvat phalasya atītena hetunā saha jātu kadācidapi saṃgatirnāsti, atītatvenobhayorapyavidyamānatvāt | nāpi ajātena hetunā atītasya phalasya saṃgatirjātu vidyate, naṣṭājātatvena ubhayorapyavidyamānatvāt, bhinnakālatvācca | nāpi jātena vartamānena hetunā saha atītasya phalasya saṃgatiḥ saṃbhavati, bhinnakālatvāt, naṣṭasya ca phalasya avidyamānatvādvandhyāputreṇeva devadattasyetyabhiprāyaḥ || 12 ||
body.translated_text: First, there is never a meeting of a past fruit with a past cause, because both are non-existent, being past. Nor is there ever a meeting of a past fruit with an unborn cause, because both are non-existent — one being destroyed and the other unborn — and because they belong to different times. Nor is a meeting of a past fruit with a born, present cause possible, because they belong to different times and because the fruit, being destroyed, is non-existent — like [the meeting of] <s>Devadatta</s> with a barren woman's son. This is the intended meaning. // 12 //

body.text: yathā ca atītasya phalasya atītena anāgatavartamānena hetunā saha na kadācit saṃgatirasti, evaṃ vartamānasyāpi phalasya traikālikena hetunā saha nāsti saṃgatiriti tat pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: And just as there is never a meeting of a past fruit with a cause of any of the three times — past, future, or present — so too is there no meeting of a present fruit with a cause of any of the three times. Demonstrating this, he says:

children.text: na jātasya hyajātena phalasya saha hetunā |
children.translated_text: There is never a meeting of a born fruit with an unborn cause, /
nor with a past [cause], nor with a born [cause]. // 13 //

body.text: jātasya phalasya bhinnakālatvādajātena ca atītena ca hetunā saha saṃgamanaṃ nāsti | nāpi vartamānasya vartamānena hetunā saha saṃgatirasti, hetuphalayoryaugapadyābhāvāt, tayośca saṃgatirvaiyarthyāt | kiṃ hi vidyamānayoḥ parasparanirapekṣayoḥ punaḥ saṃgatyā prayojanamiti nāsti saṃgatiḥ || 13 ||
body.translated_text: A born fruit has no meeting with an unborn or past cause, because they belong to different times. Nor is there a meeting of a present [fruit] with a present cause, because of the absence of simultaneity of cause and fruit, and because their meeting would be purposeless. For what purpose would meeting serve for two things that are present and mutually independent? Therefore there is no meeting. // 13 //

body.text: idānīmanāgatasyāpi phalasya yathā atītānāgatapratyutpannena hetunā saha saṃgamanaṃ nāsti tathā pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: Now, demonstrating that even of a future fruit there is no meeting with a past, future, or present cause, he says:

children.text: nājātasya hi jātena phalasya saha hetunā |
children.translated_text: For there is never any meeting of an unborn fruit
with a born cause, nor with an unborn one, nor with a perished one. // 14 //

body.text: ajātaṃ hi phalamasaṃvidyamānam | tasya bhinnakālena vartamānena atītena ca hetunā saha nāsti saṃgamanaṃ bhinnakālatvāt | anāgatenāpi hetunā saha nāsti saṃgamanam, ubhayoravidyamānatvāt || 14 ||
body.translated_text: For an unborn fruit is one that does not [yet] exist. Of that, there is no meeting with a present or past cause of a different time, because they belong to different times. Nor is there any meeting with a future cause either, since both are non-existent. // 14 //

body.text:
yadā caivaṃ sarvathā hetuphalayoḥ saṃgatirnāsti, tadā-
asatyāṃ saṃgatau hetuḥ kathaṃ janayate phalam |
body.translated_text: And when in this way there is no meeting of cause and fruit in any way whatsoever, then — in the absence of meeting, how does a cause produce a fruit?

body.text: naiva hetuḥ phalaṃ janayati saṃgateravidyamānatvāt vandhyāputramivetyabhiprāyaḥ ||
body.translated_text: The cause simply does not produce the fruit, because the meeting is non-existent — like the son of a barren woman. This is the intended meaning.

body.text: athāpi syāt- satyāmeva saṃgatau hetuḥ phalaṃ janayatīti, tadapi na yuktam, kālatraye 'pi saṃgatyanupalabdheḥ | athāpi kathaṃcid hetuphalayoḥ saṃgatiḥ parikalpyate, evamapi-
body.translated_text: Moreover, one might say: only when there is a meeting does the cause produce the fruit. But this too is not proper, since the meeting is not apprehended in any of the three times. And even if somehow the meeting of cause and fruit is imagined —

body.text: satyāṃ vā saṃgatau hetuḥ kathaṃ janayate phalam || 15 ||
body.translated_text: Or even if there is a meeting, how does the cause produce the fruit? // 15 //

body.text: saṃnihitasya phalasya punarjanmavaiyarthyāt, asaṃhitānāṃ ca saṃgaterayuktatvāt ityabhiprāyaḥ || 15 ||
body.translated_text: Because the re-production of a fruit that is already present would be pointless, and because the meeting of things that are not present together is not justified. This is the intended meaning. // 15 //

body.text: kiṃ cānyat-
body.translated_text: What is more —

children.translated_text: If the cause is empty of the fruit, how will it produce the fruit?
If the cause is non-empty of the fruit, how will it produce the fruit? // 16 //

body.text: yo 'yaṃ phalasya hetuḥ phalasya janaka iṣyate, sa tena śūnyo vā bhavan phalamutpādayet, aśūnyo vā? tatra hetuḥ śūnyaḥ phalena rahitaḥ phalaṃ na janayati, ahetuvat phalaśūnyatvāt | phalena aśūnyo 'pi hetuḥ phalaṃ na janayati, vidyamānatvāt phalasya, vidyamānaputraṃ devadatta iva | evaṃ tāvat phalaśūnyo vā phalāśūnyo vā hetuḥ phalaṃ na janayati || 16 ||
body.translated_text: This cause which is accepted as the producer of the fruit — would it produce the fruit being empty of it, or being non-empty of it? In the first case, the cause that is empty [of the fruit], i.e. devoid of the fruit, does not produce the fruit, since being empty of the fruit it is like a non-cause. And the cause that is non-empty of the fruit, too, does not produce the fruit, since the fruit already exists — like <s>Devadatta</s> who already has a living son. Thus, whether empty of the fruit or non-empty of the fruit, the cause does not produce the fruit. // 16 //

body.text: yaccāpi phalamutpadyate, taccāpyaśūnyaṃ vā samutpadyate, śūnyaṃ vā? tatra tāvat-
body.translated_text: And this fruit that arises — does it arise as non-empty or as empty? On the first point —

children.translated_text: A non-empty fruit will not arise; a non-empty [fruit] will not cease.
That non-empty [fruit], being unceased and unarisen, will be [permanent]. // 17 //

body.text: aśūnyaṃ hi phalamapratītyasamutpannaṃ svabhāvavyavasthitam, tadevaṃvidhaṃ phalaṃ naivotpatsyate svabhāvasyānapāyitvācca na nirotsyate | tataśca aśūnyaṃ tadiṣyamāṇamaniruddhamanutpannaṃ ca syāt | na caitadiṣṭam, ityataḥ aśūnyaṃ tatphalaṃ na bhavati, utpādanirodhābhyupagamāt || 17 ||
body.translated_text: For a non-empty fruit, being not dependently arisen and established by its own nature — such a fruit will never arise, and since its own nature cannot depart, it will not cease. And therefore that non-empty [fruit], as accepted, would be both unceased and unarisen. But this is not accepted — therefore that fruit is not non-empty, because arising and cessation are acknowledged. // 17 //

body.text: idānīṃ śūnyamapi tatphalaṃ na saṃbhavati, anudayāvyayavattvaprasaṅgāt iti pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: Now, demonstrating that even an empty fruit is not possible, since it would entail the consequence of non-arising and non-passing-away, he says:

children.translated_text: How will an empty [fruit] arise? How will an empty [fruit] cease?
That which is empty too, being unceased and unarisen, follows as a consequence. // 18 //

body.text: tatra śūnyamucyate yatsvabhāvena nāsti | yacca vastu svabhāvena nāsti, tat kathamutpatsyate, kathaṃ vā nirotsyate? na hi svabhāvena avidyamānasya ākāśādeḥ udayavyayau dṛṣṭau | tasmācchūnyamapi tatphalamiṣyamāṇamaniruddhamanutpannaṃ ca prasajyate || 18 ||
body.translated_text: Therein, 'empty' is said of that which does not exist by its own nature. And that entity which does not exist by its own nature — how will it arise, or how will it cease? For arising and passing away are not observed for what does not exist by its own nature, such as space and the like. Therefore, even that empty fruit, as accepted, entails the consequence of being both unceased and unarisen. // 18 //

body.text: kiṃ cānyat- yadi hetuḥ phalaṃ janayet, sa phalādavyatirikto vā janayet, vyatirikto vā? ubhayathā ca nopapadyate ityāha-
body.translated_text: What is more — if the cause were to produce the fruit, would it produce [it] as non-different from the fruit, or as different? In both ways it is untenable. Thus he says:

children.text: hetoḥ phalasya caikatvaṃ na hi jātūpapadyate |
children.translated_text: The identity of cause and fruit is never tenable.

children.text: hetoḥ phalasya cānyatvaṃ na hi jātūpapadyate || 19 ||
children.translated_text: The otherness of cause and fruit is never tenable. // 19 //

body.text: tadetat pratijñāmātrakamiti pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: Demonstrating that this is not a mere assertion, he says:

children.translated_text: If cause and fruit were identical, there would be unity of the producer and the produced.
If cause and fruit were separate, the cause would be equal to a non-cause. // 20 //

body.text: yadi hetoḥ phalasya ca ekatvaṃ syāt, tadā janyajanakayorekatvamabhyupetaṃ syāt | na cānayorekatvam, pitāputrayoścakṣuścakṣurvijñānayorbījāṅkurayoścaikyaprasaṅgāt | evaṃ tāvad hetoḥ phalasya ca ekatvaṃ nāsti ||
body.translated_text: If there were identity of cause and fruit, then the unity of the produced and the producer would be accepted. But there is no unity of these — since it would entail the absurd consequence of the identity of father and son, of the eye and eye-consciousness, and of the seed and sprout. Thus, there is no identity of cause and fruit.

body.text: idānīmanyatvamapi nāsti | kiṃ kāraṇam? yadi hetoḥ phalasya ca bhavanmatenābhimatamanyatvaṃ syāt, tadā paratra nirapekṣatvād hetunirapekṣameva phalaṃ syāt | na caitadevam, ityataḥ anyatvamapi hetoḥ phalasya ca na saṃbhavati | yayośca evaṃ vicāryamāṇayostattvānyatve na staḥ, tayorna kadācijjanyajanakabhāvaḥ iṣyate | ato naiva hetuḥ phalaṃ janayati || 20 ||
body.translated_text: Now, otherness too does not exist. For what reason? If, according to your view, there were otherness of cause and fruit, then, since [what is] other is independent of [its] counterpart, the fruit would exist independently of the cause. But this is not so — therefore otherness of cause and fruit is also not possible. And for those two, which when thus examined do not possess identity or otherness, the relationship of producer and produced is never accepted. Therefore the cause simply does not produce the fruit. // 20 //

body.text: kiṃ cānyat- yadi hetuḥ phalaṃ janayet, sa tatphalaṃ svabhāvena sadbhūtaṃ vā janayet, asadbhūtaṃ vā? ubhayathā ca na yujyate ityāha-
body.translated_text: What is more — if the cause were to produce the fruit, would it produce that fruit as truly existent by its own nature, or as truly non-existent? In both ways it is not tenable. Thus he says:

children.translated_text: What will the cause produce, if the fruit exists by its own nature?
What will the cause produce, if the fruit does not exist by its own nature? // 21 //

body.text: tatra yat phalaṃ svabhāvena sadbhūtaṃ svabhāvena vidyamānam, tanna punarjanyate vidyamānatvāt, vidyamānaghaṭavat | yadapi svabhāvena asadbhūtaṃ phalam, tadapi heturna janayati, svabhāvena asadbhūtatvāt, kharaviṣāṇavat ||
body.translated_text: Therein, a fruit that is truly existent by its own nature — i.e. existing by its own nature — is not produced again, because it already exists, like an already-existing pot. And a fruit that is truly non-existent by its own nature — that too the cause does not produce, because it is truly non-existent by its own nature, like a hare's horn.

body.text: pratibimbenānaikāntikateti cet, bhavatu anaikāntikatā, naiḥsvābhāvyaṃ tu siddhaṃ bhāvānām | tataśca sasvabhāvavādatyāgaḥ syāt, asmadvādānuvarṇanameva syāt | sasvabhāvaśca na kaścit padārtho nāma astīti pratidvandvayabhāvāt niḥsvabhāvo 'pi padārtho nāstīti kuto 'naikāntikatā? na hi asmākaṃ pratibimbakaṃ sasvabhāvaṃ nāpi niḥsvabhāvam, dharmiṇamantareṇa taddharmayorapyabhāvāt | na hi āryāḥ pratibimbakaṃ nāma kiṃcit niḥsvabhāvaṃ sasvabhāvaṃ vā upalabhanta iti ||
body.translated_text: [Objection:] The example of a reflection makes [the argument] inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>). [Reply:] Let there be inconclusiveness — still, the absence of inherent nature of entities is established. And from that, the doctrine of inherent nature would have to be abandoned, and it would amount to an endorsement of our own doctrine. And since no entity whatsoever exists with inherent nature, then due to the absence of the opponent, [the thesis] 'what is without inherent nature also does not exist as an entity' — whence the inconclusiveness? For according to us, a reflection is neither with inherent nature nor without inherent nature, since in the absence of the property-possessor (<s>dharmin</s>), its properties too are absent. For the noble ones do not apprehend anything called a 'reflection' as either with or without inherent nature.

body.text: tatra pūrvaṃ phalaṃ notpatsyate ityādinā ślokadvayena sākṣādutpattikriyākartṛtvaṃ phalasya niṣiddham | idānīṃ hetoḥ phalotpattikriyāprayojakatvaṃ pratiṣiddhamiti | ayamasya pūrvakādviśeṣa iti vijñeyam || 21 ||
body.translated_text: Therein, by the preceding two verses beginning with 'the fruit will not arise,' the fruit's being the direct agent of the action of arising was negated. Now, the cause's being the instigator of the action of the fruit's arising is negated. This should be understood as the distinction from the preceding. // 21 //

body.text: atrāha- yadyapi hetoḥ phalotpattikriyāprayojakatvaṃ niṣiddham, tathāpi hetustāvat svabhāvato 'sti, na ca asati phale hetorhetutvaṃ sidhyati, tasmāt phalamapi bhaviṣyatīti | ucyate- syāddhetuḥ, yadi ajanayato 'sya hetutvaṃ syāt |
body.translated_text: Here the opponent says: Even though the cause's being the instigator of the action of the fruit's arising has been negated, nevertheless the cause at least exists by its own nature. And since without a fruit, the cause's status as a cause is not established, therefore the fruit too will exist. [Reply:] The cause would [exist], if its status as a cause were established while not producing [anything].

body.text: na cājanayamānasya hetutvamupapadyate |
body.translated_text: But the status of a cause is not tenable for that which does not produce.

body.text: atha syāt- yadyapi evaṃ hetorhetutvaṃ nāsti, tathāpi phalaṃ tāvadasti | na ca hetumantareṇa phalaṃ yuktamiti phalasadbhāvād heturapi bhaviṣyatīti | ucyate | yadā ajanayamānasya hetorhetutvaṃ nāstītyuktam, tadā-
body.translated_text: Moreover, one might say: even though the cause's status as a cause does not exist in this way, nevertheless the fruit at least exists. And since a fruit is not proper without a cause, from the existence of the fruit, the cause too will exist. [Reply:] When it has been said that the status of a cause is not tenable for that which does not produce, then —

body.text: hetutvānupapattau ca phalaṃ kasya bhaviṣyati || 22 ||
body.translated_text: when the status of a cause is untenable, whose will the fruit be? // 22 //

body.text: iti | tasmāt phalamapi nāstīti || 22 ||
body.translated_text: Therefore the fruit too does not exist. // 22 //

body.text: atrāha- naiva hi kevalasya hetoḥ phalotpattikriyāyāḥ prayojakatvam, kiṃ tarhi hetupratyayasāmagryā phalaṃ janyate iti | ucyate | uktadoṣatvāt na yuktametat | api ca, iyaṃ hetupratyayasāmagrī yadi phalasya janiketi kalpyate, kiṃ sāsvayameva tāvadātmānaṃ janayati, utāho na? yadi janayatīti kalpyate, tanna yujyate | na hi alabdhātmabhāvasya prayojakatvaṃ dṛṣṭamityataḥ sāmagryā avaśyaṃ labdhātmabhāvayā bhavitavyam | na ca labdhātmabhāvāyāḥ punaḥ svātmotpāde prayojakatvaṃ yuktam, ityataḥ na sāmagrī svātmānamutpādayati | yā ca ātmānaṃ notpādayati, sā kathaṃ phalamutpādayituṃ śaknotīti pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: Here the opponent says: it is not the cause alone that is the instigator of the action of the fruit's arising; rather, the fruit is produced by the assemblage (<s>sāmagrī</s>) of causes and conditions. [Reply:] This is not proper, since the faults stated [above] apply. Moreover, if this assemblage of causes and conditions is imagined as the producer of the fruit — does it first produce itself, or not? If it is imagined that it produces itself, that is not tenable. For the capacity to instigate is not observed for that which has not yet attained its own existence — therefore the assemblage must necessarily have attained its own existence. But for that which has attained its own existence, the capacity to instigate its own arising again is not proper — therefore the assemblage does not produce itself. And demonstrating that what does not produce itself cannot produce a fruit, he says:

body.text: na ca pratyayahetūnāmiyamātmānamātmanā |

children.text: yā sāmagrī janayate sā kathaṃ janayetphalam |23 ||
children.translated_text: how then will it produce a fruit? // 23 //

body.translated_text: And this assemblage of conditions and causes does not produce itself;

body.text: pratyayānāṃ hetūnāṃ ca yeyaṃ sāmagrī sā tāvadātmanaiva ātmānaṃ notpādayati, svātmani vṛttivirodhāt, satyāḥ punarutpādavaiyarthyācca | yā ca evamātmānameva tāvanna janayati, sā kathaṃ phalaṃ janayiṣyati? na hi bandhyāduhitā ātmānaṃ janayitumaśaktā satī putraṃ janayiṣyatīti yujyate | evaṃ sāmagryapi svātmājanikā phalaṃ janayatīti na yujyate || 23 ||
body.translated_text: This assemblage of conditions and causes does not produce itself by itself, because of the contradiction of an action operating upon its own substrate, and because when it already exists, its re-arising would be pointless. And that which in this way does not even produce itself — how will it produce a fruit? For it is not proper that a daughter of a barren woman, being unable to produce herself, should produce a son. Likewise, it is not proper that the assemblage too, being non-productive of itself, should produce a fruit. // 23 //

body.text: tasmāt-
body.translated_text: Therefore —

body.text: na sāmagrīkṛtaṃ phalaṃ
body.translated_text: the fruit is not produced by the assemblage.

body.text: athāpi syāt- yadi sāmagrīkṛtaṃ phalaṃ na saṃbhavati, evaṃ tarhi asāmagrīkṛtaṃ bhaviṣyatīti cet, ucyate-
body.translated_text: Moreover, one might say: if a fruit produced by the assemblage is not possible, then it will be produced without an assemblage. [Reply:] —

children.translated_text: Nor is the fruit produced without an assemblage.

children.text: yadā sāmagrīkṛtaṃ phalaṃ na saṃbhavati, tadā kathamatyantaviruddhamasāmagrīkṛtaṃ bhaviṣyati? asāmagrīkṛtaṃ phalaṃ na saṃbhavati ||
children.translated_text: When a fruit produced by the assemblage is not possible, how could one that is utterly contradictory — produced without an assemblage — come to be? A fruit produced without an assemblage is not possible.

body.text: atha syāt- yadyapi nāsti phalaṃ svabhāvataḥ, tathāpi hetupratyayasāmagrī tāvadasti | na ca phalamantareṇa hetupratyayasāmagrī saṃbhavatīti phalamapi saṃbhaviṣyatīti | ucyate | syāddhetupratyayasāmagrī, yadi phalameva bhavet | yadā tu yathoditena nyāyena phalameva nāsti, tadā-
body.translated_text: Moreover, one might say: even though the fruit does not exist by its own nature, the assemblage of causes and conditions at least exists. And since the assemblage of causes and conditions is not possible without a fruit, the fruit too will exist. [Reply:] The assemblage of causes and conditions would [exist], if only the fruit were to exist. But when, by the reasoning stated above, the fruit itself does not exist, then —

body.text: asti pratyayasāmagrī kuta eva phalaṃ vinā || 24 ||
body.translated_text: how could the assemblage of conditions exist without the fruit? // 24 //

body.text: phalābhāve sati nirhetukā hetupratyayasāmagrī api nāstītyabhiprāyaḥ | uktaṃ hi āryalalitavistarasūtre-
body.translated_text: In the absence of the fruit, the assemblage of causes and conditions too, being causeless, does not exist. This is the intended meaning. For it is stated in the noble <s>Lalitavistara Sūtra</s>:

children.text: kaṇṭhoṣṭha pratītya tālukaṃ jihvaparivarti ravanti akṣarāḥ |
children.translated_text: Dependent on the throat, lips, palate, and the turning of the tongue, syllables resound.

children.text: na ca kaṇṭhagatā na tāluke akṣaraikaikaśa nopalabhyate ||
children.translated_text: But they are not in the throat, not in the palate — each syllable individually is not apprehended.

children.text: sāmagri pratītyataśca sā vāca manabuddhivaśena niścarī |
children.translated_text: Dependent on the assemblage, that speech issues forth under the power of mind and intellect.
Mind and speech are of invisible form — they are not apprehended either externally or internally.
The wise one who sees the arising and passing away of the sound, note, and tone of speech,

children.text: kṣaṇikāṃ vaśikāṃ tadā dṛśī sarva vāca pratiśrutakopamā ||
children.translated_text: sees that all speech is momentary, under [one's own] control, and like an echo. //

body.text: tathā āryopāliparipṛcchāyāmuktaṃ bhagavatā-
body.translated_text: Likewise, it is stated by the <s>Bhagavān</s> in the noble <s>Upāliparipṛcchā</s>:

body.text:
iha śāsani sūramaṇīye pravrajathā gṛhiliṅga jahitvā |
phalavantu bhaviṣyatha śreṣṭhā eṣu nideśitu kāruṇikena |
body.translated_text: Go forth into this excellent, heroic dispensation, having abandoned the householder's garb! You shall become fruitful, O excellent ones, as instructed by the Compassionate One.

children.text: pravrajitva gṛhiliṅga jahitvā sarvaphalasya bhaviṣyati prāptiḥ |
children.translated_text: Having gone forth and abandoned the householder's garb, there will be attainment of all fruits.

children.text: puna dharmasabhāva tulitvā sarvaphalāna phalāna ca prāptiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Then, having weighed the nature of <s>dharmas</s>, there will be attainment of all fruits and of the fruits [of the path].

body.text:
alabhanta phalaṃ tatha prāptiṃ āścariyaṃ puna jāyati teṣām |
aho 'tikāruṇiko narasiṃho suṣṭupadeśita yukti jinena || iti |
body.translated_text: They obtained the fruit and the attainment — and again wonder arises for them: 'Ah, how supremely compassionate is the Lion among Men! Well taught is the method by the <s>Jina</s>!' //

body.text: tathā āryaprajñāpāramitāyāmaṣṭasāhasrikāyām-
body.translated_text: Likewise, in the noble <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s> in Eight Thousand [Lines]:

body.text: tena hi kauśika bodhisattvena mahāsattvena mahāsaṃnāhasaṃnaddhena na rūpe sthātavyaṃ na vedanāyāṃ na saṃjñāyāṃ na saṃskāreṣu na vijñāne sthātavyam | na srotaāpattiphale na sakṛdāgāmiphale na anāgāmiphale na arhattve na pratyekabuddhatve na samyaksaṃbuddhatve sthātavyam || iti ||
body.translated_text: 'Therefore, <s>Kauśika</s>, the <s>Bodhisattva Mahāsattva</s> who has donned the great armor should not stand in form, should not stand in feeling, in perception, in formations, or in consciousness. He should not stand in the fruit of stream-entry, in the fruit of once-returning, in the fruit of non-returning, in <s>Arhatship</s>, in <s>Pratyekabuddhahood</s>, or in perfect complete awakening (<s>samyaksaṃbodhitva</s>).'

body.text: ityācāryacandrakīrtipādoparacitāyāṃ prasannapadāyāṃ madhyamakavṛttau sāmagrīparīkṣā nāma viṃśatitamaṃ prakaraṇam ||
body.translated_text: Thus ends the twentieth chapter, 'Examination of the Assemblage' (<s>Sāmagrīparīkṣā</s>), in the <s>Prasannapadā</s>, the <s>Madhyamaka</s> commentary composed by the venerable <s>Ācārya Candrakīrti</s>. //

body.text:
21
saṃbhavavibhavaparīkṣā ekaviṃśatitamaṃ prakaraṇam |
body.translated_text:
21
'Examination of Arising and Destruction' (<s>Saṃbhavavibhavaparīkṣā</s>), the twenty-first chapter.

body.text: atrāha- vidyata eva svabhāvataḥ kālaḥ, saṃbhavavibhavanimittatvāt | iha kaṃcit kālaviśeṣamapekṣya aṅkurotpattiḥ bhāvānāmutpādo bhavati, kaṃcitkālaviśeṣamapekṣya vibhavo vināśo bhavati, na sarvadā, vidyamānāyāmapi hetupratyayasāmagryām- ityato vidyata eva kālaḥ, saṃbhavavibhava nimittattvāt | ucyate | syāt saṃbhavavibhavanimittatā kālasya yadi saṃbhavavibhavāveva syātām | na tu staḥ | yathā ca na staḥ, tathā pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: Here the opponent says: Time does indeed exist by its own nature, because it is the cause of arising and destruction. Here, in dependence on a particular time, the arising of entities — such as the sprout's arising — occurs; and in dependence on a particular time, destruction occurs — not at all times, even when the aggregate of causes and conditions is present. Therefore time does exist, because it is the cause of arising and destruction. [Reply:] Time would be the cause of arising and destruction if arising and destruction themselves existed. But they do not. And to demonstrate how they do not, he says:

children.text: vinā vā saha vā nāsti vibhavaḥ saṃbhavena vai |
children.translated_text: Destruction does not exist either without or together with arising. /

children.text: vinā vā saha vā nāsti saṃbhavo vibhavena vai || 1 ||
children.translated_text: Arising does not exist either without or together with destruction. // 1 //

body.text: iha yadi saṃbhavavibhavau syātām, tau anyonyaṃ sahabhāvena vā syātām, vinābhāvena vā | ubhayathā ca vicāryamāṇau na saṃbhavataḥ | kathaṃ kṛtvā? tatra tāvad yathā vinā saṃbhavena utpādena vibhavo vināśo nāsti, tathā pratipādayannāha-
body.translated_text: Here, if arising and destruction existed, they would exist either simultaneously with each other or separately. And when examined in both ways, they are not possible. How so? Therein, first, to demonstrate that destruction does not exist without arising:

children.text: bhaviṣyati kathaṃ nāma vibhavaḥ saṃbhavaṃ vinā |
children.translated_text: How could there possibly be destruction without arising? /

children.text: vinaiva janma maraṇaṃ vibhavo nodbhavaṃ vinā || 2 ||
children.translated_text: There is no death without birth; destruction does not exist without coming-into-being. // 2 //
